bio_edx.1.1.summary: Mitosis is the type of cell division that makes two **genetically identical diploid daughter cells** from one parent cell. Organisms rely on it for three jobs: **growth** (making more cells so the organism gets bigger), **repair** (replacing damaged, worn-out or dead cells) and **asexual reproduction** (making offspring from one parent that are clones of that parent). In every case the reason mitosis is used is the same: the new cells must carry exactly the same genetic information as the cells they came from.

core.h: The big idea: why organisms need mitosis
core.p: A multicellular organism starts life as one cell, a fertilised egg (zygote). To become an adult made of millions or billions of cells, that one cell and its descendants must divide again and again. The type of division used is **mitosis**. Edexcel expects you to describe the **importance of mitosis in growth, repair and asexual reproduction**.
bullets: Mitosis produces **two daughter cells** from one parent cell.
The daughter cells are **genetically identical** to each other and to the parent cell.
The daughter cells are **diploid**: they have two sets of chromosomes, just like the parent cell.
Because every new cell has the full, correct set of genes, it can do the same job as the cell it replaces or sits next to.
The three roles to learn are **growth**, **repair** and **asexual reproduction**.

callouts.p: A type of cell division that produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells from one parent cell.
Growth, repair and asexual reproduction. Learn all three: a 3 mark question often gives one mark for each.

core.h: What makes mitosis suitable for these jobs
core.p: You do not need the stages of mitosis for this point, but you do need the outcome, because the outcome explains the importance. Before a cell divides, its DNA is copied, so each chromosome is duplicated. Mitosis then shares the copies out equally, so each daughter cell receives one complete copy of every chromosome.
bullets: Same **number** of chromosomes in each daughter cell as in the parent cell (in humans, 46).
Same **genes and alleles** in each daughter cell, so the cells are genetically identical.
Both daughter cells are **diploid** body cells.
No genetic variation is produced by mitosis itself. Variation only appears if a mutation happens.
This is exactly what is needed when the aim is 'more of the same': more body cells, replacement cells, or copies of a whole organism.

head: Feature of mitosis
Why it matters
rows: Two daughter cells from one parent cell
The number of cells increases, so tissue can grow or be replaced
New cells have the same genes, so they work in the same way as the original cells
Each new body cell keeps the full two sets of chromosomes
One cell can become millions of cells

callouts.p: A cell that has two sets of chromosomes (one set from each parent). Human diploid body cells have 46 chromosomes, in 23 pairs.

core.p: **Growth** is a permanent increase in the size or mass of an organism. In multicellular organisms the main way of growing is by increasing the **number of cells**, and those extra cells are made by mitosis.
bullets: A zygote divides by mitosis to form a ball of cells called an embryo, and division carries on as the embryo develops into a fetus, a baby, a child and then an adult.
Each division doubles the cell number: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and so on.
Every body cell produced has the same 46 chromosomes as the zygote (in humans), so all body cells contain the same genetic information.
In animals, growth by mitosis happens all over the body while the animal is young, then mostly stops when adult size is reached.
In plants, cell division by mitosis carries on throughout life at the tips of roots and shoots.
Without mitosis an organism would stay as a single cell and could not become large or complex.

callouts.p: In an exam answer on growth, say that mitosis **increases the number of cells**. Do not say that cells simply 'get bigger'.
Cell elongation and differentiation are also part of growth, but they belong to a different spec point. For this point, the link you need is mitosis makes more cells.

core.p: Cells do not last for ever. Some are damaged by injury, some simply wear out and die, and some are lost from the body surface every day. **Mitosis makes new cells to replace them**, so that tissues keep working.
bullets: When you cut your skin, cells near the wound divide by mitosis to make new skin cells that fill the gap.
Skin cells are constantly rubbed off the surface and replaced by mitosis of cells underneath.
Cells lining the gut are worn away by food passing through and are replaced by mitosis.
Red blood cells only last a few months. New ones are made by mitosis of cells in the bone marrow.
A broken bone heals because bone cells divide by mitosis to make new bone tissue.
Plants also repair damage: cells divide by mitosis to cover a wound in a stem.

callouts.t: Why identical cells matter for repair
callouts.p: The replacement cells must be genetically identical to the cells that were lost so that they carry the same genes, can carry out the same function and fit into the tissue.

Mark schemes accept 'repair of damaged tissue' or 'replacement of damaged, dead or worn-out cells'. Writing 'mitosis repairs cells' is weaker: mitosis makes **new cells**, it does not mend broken ones.

core.p: **Asexual reproduction** needs only **one parent**. There are no gametes and no fertilisation. Cells of the parent divide by mitosis, and some of the new cells become a new individual. Because mitosis makes genetically identical cells, the offspring are genetically identical to the parent and to each other: they are **clones**.
bullets: Only one parent is needed, so there is no need to find a mate.
There is no fusion of gametes, so there is no mixing of genetic information from two parents.
All the cells of the offspring are made by mitosis from cells of the parent.
The offspring are **genetically identical** to the parent (clones).
Any differences between parent and offspring are caused by the environment or by mutation, not by the way they were produced.

callouts.p: Reproduction involving only one parent, without gametes or fertilisation, producing offspring that are genetically identical to the parent (clones).
An organism (or cell) that is genetically identical to its parent.

core.h: Examples of asexual reproduction by mitosis
core.p: Exam questions often describe an organism you may not have met and ask you to explain how you know the offspring are genetically identical. Whatever the example, the answer is the same: the offspring were produced by mitosis from one parent.
bullets: **Strawberry plants** grow side stems called runners. Where a runner touches the soil, a new plant grows by mitosis.
**Potato plants** form tubers. Each tuber can grow into a new plant that is genetically identical to the parent plant.
**Daffodils** form bulbs that produce new identical plants.
**Spider plants** produce small plantlets on long stems.
**Yeast** (a single-celled fungus) reproduces by budding: a new cell grows out of the parent cell.
Gardeners take **cuttings** from a plant. The cutting grows roots by mitosis and becomes a clone of the original plant.

head: Organism
How it reproduces asexually
Result
rows: New cells identical to parent cell

callouts.p: Bacteria reproduce asexually by binary fission. They have no nucleus, so do not call this mitosis in an exam answer.

core.h: Why asexual reproduction by mitosis is useful, and its cost
core.p: Because the offspring are clones, asexual reproduction has clear benefits and one big risk. You only need the outline here to explain why identical offspring matter.
bullets: It is **fast**: only one parent is needed and no time or energy is spent finding a mate.
Many offspring can be produced quickly when conditions are good.
If the parent is well suited to its environment, the identical offspring will be well suited too.
The cost is that there is **no genetic variation** in the offspring.
If the environment changes, for example a new disease arrives, all the clones are likely to be affected in the same way and the whole population could die.

callouts.t: Link the idea back to mitosis
callouts.p: No variation in the offspring is a direct result of mitosis producing genetically identical cells.

core.p: The three roles use exactly the same process. What differs is the purpose and what happens to the new cells.
bullets: Growth: new cells are **added**, so the total number of cells in the organism goes up.
Repair: new cells **replace** cells that were lost, so the number of cells is restored.
Asexual reproduction: new cells form a **separate new organism**.

head: Role
What mitosis does
Example
rows: Increases the number of cells so the organism gets bigger
A zygote developing into an embryo
Makes new cells to replace damaged, worn-out or dead cells
Makes the cells of a new organism from one parent
Strawberry runner forming a new plant

callouts.p: **GRA**: Growth, Repair, Asexual reproduction.

core.p: Because each cell divides into two, the number of cells doubles with every round of mitosis. Edexcel can ask you to calculate cell numbers.
bullets: Starting from one cell: number of cells after n divisions = 2^n (2 to the power n).
After 1 division: 2 cells. After 2: 4 cells. After 3: 8 cells. After 10: 1024 cells.
Starting from more than one cell: number of cells = starting number x 2^n.
To find the number of divisions, divide the total time by the time for one division.
Real tissues do not double for ever: division is controlled, and cells also die.

callouts.p: After 5 divisions there are 32 cells, not 10. Each division multiplies the number of cells by 2.

core.h: Mitosis is not used to make gametes
core.p: To see why mitosis matters, it helps to know what it is not used for. Gametes (sperm and egg cells, pollen and ovules) are made by a different type of division, meiosis, which makes haploid cells that are genetically different. Mitosis makes **body cells**.
bullets: Mitosis: growth, repair, asexual reproduction. Two identical diploid cells.
Gametes are not made by mitosis.
After fertilisation, the zygote divides by **mitosis**, so growth of the embryo is a mitosis role.

callouts.p: Write mitosis clearly. An answer that looks like a mixture of 'mitosis' and 'meiosis' will not be given the mark.

core.p: Questions on this point are usually 'state', 'describe' or 'explain' questions worth 1 to 4 marks, often attached to a context such as a wound healing or a plant producing runners.
bullets: Name the process: **mitosis**.
State the product: **two genetically identical diploid daughter cells**.
Link to the context: growth (more cells), repair (replace damaged cells) or asexual reproduction (offspring are clones).
For 'explain why the offspring are identical', say they were produced by mitosis from **one parent**, with no gametes or fertilisation, so there is no mixing of genetic information.
Use 'genetically identical' rather than just 'the same'.

callouts.p: 'State' needs a short fact. 'Describe' needs what happens. 'Explain' needs a reason, so include 'because' or 'so that'.

analogy.p: Mitosis is like a photocopier that makes exact copies of one master document. If the office needs more copies because it is expanding, it photocopies more (growth). If a copy gets torn or coffee-stained, it photocopies a replacement (repair). If a new branch office opens, it is given a complete identical set of documents (asexual reproduction). In every case the copy must match the original exactly. Where it breaks down: a photocopier leaves the original untouched and makes a separate copy, but in mitosis the parent cell itself divides and becomes the two daughter cells, so there is no 'original' left afterwards. Also, cells copy their own DNA; no outside machine does it for them.

terms.d: Cell division that produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells from one parent cell.
The two new cells produced when a parent cell divides.
The cell that divides to produce daughter cells.
Having exactly the same genes and alleles (the same DNA).
Having two sets of chromosomes. Human diploid cells have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs).
A long molecule of DNA, found in the nucleus, that carries genes.
A permanent increase in the size or mass of an organism, mainly by an increase in the number of cells.
The replacement of damaged, worn-out or dead cells with new cells produced by mitosis.
Reproduction from one parent without gametes or fertilisation, producing genetically identical offspring.
An organism or cell that is genetically identical to its parent.
A fertilised egg cell. It is diploid and divides by mitosis to form an embryo.
The ball of cells produced when a zygote divides repeatedly by mitosis.
A side stem of a plant such as a strawberry that grows along the ground and forms new plants asexually.
Any cell of a multicellular organism that is not a gamete. Body cells are diploid and are made by mitosis.
Differences in the genetic information of individuals. Mitosis does not produce it.

mistakes.w: Mitosis makes cells grow bigger.
mistakes.r: Mitosis increases the **number** of cells. Growth happens because there are more cells.

mistakes.w: Mitosis repairs damaged cells.
mistakes.r: Mitosis produces **new cells** that **replace** damaged or dead cells; it does not mend the damaged cell.

mistakes.w: The daughter cells are similar to the parent cell.
mistakes.r: The daughter cells are **genetically identical** to the parent cell and to each other.

mistakes.w: Mitosis produces haploid cells.
mistakes.r: Mitosis produces **diploid** cells with the same number of chromosomes as the parent cell.

mistakes.w: Mitosis is used to make gametes.
mistakes.r: Gametes are made by meiosis. Mitosis is used for growth, repair and asexual reproduction.

mistakes.w: Asexual reproduction needs two parents of the same type.
mistakes.r: Asexual reproduction needs only **one parent**; there are no gametes and no fertilisation.

mistakes.w: After 4 divisions one cell has made 8 cells.
mistakes.r: The number doubles each time: 2, 4, 8, 16. After 4 divisions there are 16 cells (2^4).

mistakes.w: Offspring from asexual reproduction show variation because they grow in different places.
mistakes.r: They are genetically identical clones. Any differences are due to the environment, not their genes.

exam.q: State the type of cell division used for growth and repair.
model: Mitosis
exam.tip: Spell it clearly so it cannot be confused with meiosis.

exam.q: State three roles of mitosis in living organisms.
model: Growth
Repair (replacement of damaged or worn-out cells)
Asexual reproduction
exam.tip: One word or phrase per mark is enough for a 'state' question.

exam.q: Describe the cells produced when one cell divides by mitosis.
model: Two daughter cells are produced
They are genetically identical (to each other and to the parent cell) / they are diploid
exam.tip: Number of cells and 'genetically identical' are the two most common marking points.

exam.q: A student cuts their finger. Explain how mitosis helps the skin to heal.
model: Skin cells (near the cut) divide by mitosis to produce new cells
The new cells are genetically identical, so they replace the damaged cells and carry out the same function
exam.tip: Say 'replace' and link identical cells to doing the same job.

exam.q: A strawberry plant produces new plants on runners. Explain why the new plants are genetically identical to the parent plant.
model: This is asexual reproduction / there is only one parent
There are no gametes and no fertilisation, so no mixing of genetic information
The cells of the new plants are produced by mitosis, which makes genetically identical cells
exam.tip: Three marks, three ideas: one parent, no fertilisation, mitosis.

exam.q: Explain why mitosis is important for the growth of a human embryo from a zygote.
model: Mitosis increases the number of cells
Each new cell is genetically identical / has the same (diploid) number of chromosomes as the zygote
exam.tip: Growth answers need the idea of more cells.

exam.q: A single cell divides by mitosis every 12 hours. Calculate the number of cells present after 3 days.
model: Number of divisions = 72 / 12 = 6
Number of cells = 2^6 = 64
exam.tip: Convert days to hours first, then double once for each division.

exam.q: Give one reason why it is important that cells produced for repair are genetically identical to the cells they replace.
model: So that they have the same genes and can carry out the same function as the cells they replace
exam.tip: Function is the key idea.

exam.q: A farmer grows a field of potato plants from tubers taken from one parent plant. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of the plants being produced by asexual reproduction.
model: Advantage: all plants are genetically identical to the parent
so they will all have the parent's desirable characteristics / reproduction is fast as only one parent is needed
Disadvantage: there is no genetic variation between the plants
so a disease (or change in conditions) that affects one plant is likely to affect them all
exam.tip: For each point give the statement and then the consequence.

exam.q: Explain the importance of mitosis in the life of a multicellular organism such as a strawberry plant.
model: Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells from one parent cell
Growth: mitosis increases the number of cells so the plant gets bigger, for example at the tips of roots and shoots
All the cells of the plant therefore contain the same genetic information
Repair: mitosis produces new cells to replace damaged or dead cells, for example where a stem is wounded
The replacement cells are identical so they can carry out the same function
Asexual reproduction: cells divide by mitosis to form new plants on runners, from one parent with no gametes or fertilisation
The new plants are clones, genetically identical to the parent
exam.tip: Structure a 6 mark answer around the three roles and link each one to 'genetically identical cells'.

worked.q: One cell divides by mitosis once every 24 hours. How many cells will there be after 5 days, assuming every cell keeps dividing and none die?
steps: Find the number of divisions: 5 days x 24 hours = 120 hours; 120 / 24 = 5 divisions.
Each division doubles the number of cells, so number of cells = 2^5.
worked.ans: 32 cells

worked.q: A sample of tissue contains 500 cells. Each cell divides by mitosis every 8 hours. Calculate the number of cells after 24 hours.
steps: Number of divisions = 24 / 8 = 3.
Each division doubles the number, so multiply by 2^3 = 8.
worked.ans: 4000 cells

worked.q: Model answer: A gardener takes a cutting from a rose plant with red flowers. Explain why the plant that grows from the cutting also has red flowers.
steps: Identify the process: growing a plant from a cutting is asexual reproduction, with one parent.
State how the new cells are made: the cells of the cutting divide by mitosis to make roots and new shoots.
State the product of mitosis: the new cells are genetically identical to the cells of the parent plant.
Link to the question: the new plant has the same genes (alleles) for flower colour as the parent, so its flowers are also red.
worked.ans: The new plant is a clone produced by mitosis, so it has the same alleles for flower colour as the parent.

bio_edx.1.10.summary: A **reflex** is a rapid, automatic response to a stimulus that does not involve the conscious part of the brain. The pathway the electrical impulses take is called a **reflex arc**: receptor, **sensory neurone**, **relay neurone** in the central nervous system, **motor neurone**, effector. Because the arc uses very few neurones and misses out conscious thought, the response is fast enough to protect the body from harm.

core.p: Most of what you do is **voluntary**: you decide to do it, using the conscious part of your brain. A **reflex** is different. It happens automatically, without you having to think, and it happens very quickly.
bullets: A reflex is **rapid**: the response happens in a fraction of a second.
A reflex is **automatic (involuntary)**: you do not decide to do it and it does not need conscious thought.
The same stimulus always produces the same response.
Reflexes are **protective**: they help prevent injury or help the body work safely.
Reflexes do not have to be learned: a newborn baby already has them.

callouts.p: A rapid, automatic response to a stimulus that does not involve the conscious part of the brain.
The pathway of neurones that an electrical impulse travels along in a reflex: receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector.

core.p: The function of a reflex arc is to produce a response quickly enough to protect the body. If you had to think about pulling your hand off a hot pan, the extra time would mean a worse burn.
bullets: Pulling a hand away from a hot or sharp object reduces damage to the skin.
Blinking when something comes towards the eye protects the surface of the eye.
The pupil getting smaller in bright light protects the light-sensitive cells of the retina from damage.
Coughing or sneezing clears the airways.
Reflexes therefore increase the chance of survival.

head: Reflex
Stimulus
Effector
Response
How it protects
rows: Hot or sharp object touching skin

callouts.p: If asked why a reflex is important, write that it is a rapid response that protects the body from harm or damage, then say what the harm would be in that example.

core.h: The five parts of a reflex arc
core.p: A reflex arc links a receptor to an effector through the central nervous system using just three neurones. The CNS is the brain and spinal cord; many reflexes, such as the withdrawal reflex, pass through the **spinal cord**.
bullets: **Receptor**: cells that detect the stimulus and generate an electrical impulse.
**Sensory neurone**: carries the impulse from the receptor to the CNS.
**Relay neurone**: a short neurone inside the CNS that passes the impulse from the sensory neurone to the motor neurone.
**Motor neurone**: carries the impulse from the CNS to the effector.
**Effector**: a muscle or gland that produces the response. A muscle contracts; a gland releases (secretes) a substance.

callouts.p: stimulus -> receptor -> sensory neurone -> relay neurone -> motor neurone -> effector -> response

callouts.t: Stimulus and response are not parts of the arc
callouts.p: The stimulus is the change that starts the reflex and the response is what happens at the end. The structures of the arc are the receptor, the three neurones and the effector.

core.h: Worked through: touching a hot object
core.p: The withdrawal reflex is the example most often used in exam questions. Be ready to describe each step with the correct structure named.
bullets: **Stimulus**: the high temperature of the object.
**Receptors** in the skin of the finger detect the stimulus and generate electrical impulses.
Impulses travel along a **sensory neurone** from the finger to the spinal cord.
In the spinal cord the signal crosses a **synapse** to a **relay neurone**.
The signal crosses a second synapse from the relay neurone to a **motor neurone**.
Impulses travel along the motor neurone out of the spinal cord to the **effector**, a muscle in the arm.
**Response**: the muscle contracts and the hand is pulled away.

callouts.p: If the question is about a different reflex, keep the same order of neurones but change the receptor, the effector and the response to fit the example given.

core.p: The three neurones in a reflex arc do not touch. There is a **synapse** between the sensory neurone and the relay neurone, and another between the relay neurone and the motor neurone.
bullets: When an impulse reaches the end of a neurone, a **neurotransmitter** is released.
The neurotransmitter **diffuses across the gap** and binds to receptors on the next neurone.
This generates a **new electrical impulse** in the next neurone.
Synapses make sure the impulse can only go one way round the arc: from sensory to relay to motor.
Each synapse slows the signal slightly, because diffusion takes time.

callouts.p: A reflex arc has only a small number of synapses. This is one reason why a reflex is faster than a voluntary action.

core.p: Explaining the speed of a reflex is a common 2 or 3 mark question. There are two linked reasons.
bullets: The impulse **does not pass through the conscious part of the brain**, so no time is spent on thinking and deciding.
The pathway is **short and uses only three neurones**, so there are few synapses to delay the signal.
Along each neurone the signal is an electrical impulse, which travels very quickly.
In a voluntary action the impulse has to travel up to the brain, pass through many more neurones and synapses there, and then travel back down, which takes longer.
The faster the response, the less time the harmful stimulus has to cause damage.

callouts.t: Do not say 'the brain is not involved'
callouts.p: Some reflexes, such as blinking and the pupil reflex, do pass through the brain. The safe phrase is that a reflex does not involve the CONSCIOUS part of the brain.

core.h: Reflex actions compared with voluntary actions
core.p: Examiners like you to compare the two kinds of response. A comparison needs a statement about each.
bullets: A reflex is automatic; a voluntary action is under conscious control.
A reflex is faster; a voluntary action is slower.
A reflex gives the same response every time; a voluntary response can be different each time.
A reflex arc is coordinated by a relay neurone in the spinal cord or unconscious part of the brain; a voluntary action is coordinated by the conscious part of the brain.

head: Feature
Reflex action
Voluntary action
rows: Pulling hand from a hot object

core.h: Why you feel the pain after you have moved
core.p: When you touch something hot, your hand moves and then, a moment later, you feel the pain. This fits the idea of the reflex arc.
bullets: In the spinal cord, the sensory neurone also passes the signal to other neurones that carry impulses **up to the brain**.
That route is longer and has more synapses, so the information reaches the conscious part of the brain **after** the reflex response has started.
This is how you become aware of what happened, and can then choose what to do next, such as running the burn under cold water.
The brain can sometimes send impulses down to override a reflex, for example holding on to a hot plate so you do not drop it. That is a conscious decision, not part of the reflex arc.

callouts.p: Being aware of a reflex does not mean the conscious brain caused it. The response is produced by the reflex arc; the awareness arrives by a separate, slower route.

core.p: Exam papers often show a section through the spinal cord with three neurones and ask you to name them or to draw arrows showing the direction of the impulse.
bullets: The neurone coming **from the receptor into** the spinal cord is the **sensory neurone**. Its cell body is part-way along, on a side branch.
The small neurone **entirely inside** the spinal cord is the **relay neurone**.
The neurone going **out of the spinal cord to a muscle or gland** is the **motor neurone**. Its cell body is at the end inside the spinal cord.
Arrows go from the receptor, along the sensory neurone, through the relay neurone, along the motor neurone, to the effector.
The gaps where the neurones meet are synapses.

callouts.t: Follow the route with your pencil
callouts.p: Start at the receptor and trace to the effector. The first neurone you travel along is sensory, the last is motor, and the one in the middle is the relay neurone.

core.h: Reflexes with a gland as the effector
core.p: Effectors are not always muscles. In some reflexes the effector is a **gland**, and the response is the release of a substance.
bullets: The arc is exactly the same: receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector.
Example: food in the mouth is the stimulus, and salivary glands respond by releasing saliva.
In the answer, write that the gland **releases** or **secretes** the substance, not that it contracts.
Whatever the effector, it is always the **motor neurone** that carries the impulse to it.

callouts.p: A muscle or gland that brings about a response to a stimulus.

core.p: You can be asked to use data about the length of a reflex arc and the speed of impulses. Use time = distance / speed, and add any delay at synapses.
bullets: speed = distance / time, so time = distance / speed.
Make sure distance is in metres and speed in metres per second, so the time is in seconds.
1 s = 1000 ms, so multiply seconds by 1000 to give milliseconds.
Total time for the arc = time along the neurones + total delay at the synapses.
The measured time for a real response is longer still, because the muscle also takes time to contract.

callouts.p: Check whether the question wants seconds or milliseconds, and give the unit with your answer.

analogy.t: The fire alarm that sets off the sprinklers
analogy.p: In a building, a heat sensor (receptor) is wired (sensory neurone) to a local control box on the same floor (relay neurone in the spinal cord), which is wired (motor neurone) straight to the sprinklers (effector). The sprinklers come on at once. A message is also sent to the manager's office at the top of the building (the conscious brain), but nobody waits for the manager to read it and decide: by the time the manager knows, the water is already flowing. That is why the response is fast and always the same. Where it breaks down: wires carry a continuous electric current, while neurones carry separate electrical impulses and pass the signal between them chemically across synapses; and a real person can sometimes consciously override a reflex, which a simple sprinkler circuit cannot do.

terms.d: A rapid, automatic response to a stimulus that does not involve the conscious part of the brain.
The pathway of neurones taken by impulses in a reflex: receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector.
A change in the environment that is detected by receptors.
A cell that detects a stimulus and generates an electrical impulse.
A neurone that carries impulses from a receptor to the central nervous system.
A short neurone in the central nervous system that links a sensory neurone to a motor neurone.
A neurone that carries impulses from the central nervous system to an effector.
A muscle or gland that brings about a response.
The action that results from a stimulus, such as a muscle contracting or a gland releasing a substance.
The brain and spinal cord.
The part of the CNS that runs down the back inside the backbone; many reflex arcs pass through it.
The gap between two neurones, crossed by a neurotransmitter.
A chemical that diffuses across a synapse and causes a new impulse in the next neurone.
Happening without conscious thought or decision.
A response that is under conscious control and is coordinated by the conscious part of the brain.

mistakes.w: A reflex does not involve the brain.
mistakes.r: A reflex does not involve the CONSCIOUS part of the brain. Some reflexes do pass through the brain.

mistakes.w: The order is receptor, motor neurone, relay neurone, sensory neurone, effector.
mistakes.r: Sensory comes first and motor last: receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector.

mistakes.w: A message is sent to the muscle.
mistakes.r: An electrical impulse travels along the motor neurone to the effector (muscle).

mistakes.w: The relay neurone is in the brain where you decide what to do.
mistakes.r: The relay neurone links the sensory and motor neurones in the CNS (for example the spinal cord). No decision is made in a reflex.

mistakes.w: Reflexes are fast because the impulses travel faster.
mistakes.r: Reflexes are fast because the pathway is short, with few neurones and synapses, and it does not go through the conscious part of the brain.

mistakes.w: The effector is the hand moving away.
mistakes.r: The effector is the muscle (or gland). The hand moving away is the response.

mistakes.w: The receptor is the hot object.
mistakes.r: The hot object (its temperature) is the stimulus. The receptor is the cell in the skin that detects it.

mistakes.w: The muscle relaxes to pull the hand away.
mistakes.r: The muscle contracts to bring about the response.

mistakes.w: Reflexes are important because they are quick.
mistakes.r: Give the reason the speed matters: a rapid response protects the body from harm or damage.

exam.q: State what is meant by the term reflex.
model: A rapid / fast response (to a stimulus).
That is automatic / involuntary / does not involve the conscious part of the brain.
exam.tip: Two ideas are needed: speed and automatic.

exam.q: Name the neurone that carries impulses from the central nervous system to an effector.
model: Motor neurone.
exam.tip: Motor = moves the muscle.

exam.q: Which type of neurone is found only in the central nervous system?
model: Relay neurone.
exam.tip: It relays the impulse between the other two.

exam.q: Give the order of the structures an impulse passes through in a reflex arc, starting with the receptor.
model: Receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone
then motor neurone, effector (all in correct order).
exam.tip: Write the full chain with arrows; one item out of place loses a mark.

exam.q: A person touches a hot plate and pulls their hand away. Identify the stimulus, the effector and the response in this reflex.
model: Stimulus: the heat / high temperature of the plate.
Effector: muscle (in the arm).
Response: the muscle contracts / the hand is pulled away.
exam.tip: The effector is always a muscle or gland, never the action itself.

exam.q: Explain why a reflex response is faster than a voluntary response.
model: The impulse does not travel to / is not processed by the conscious part of the brain.
So the pathway is shorter / there are fewer neurones and synapses to cross.
exam.tip: Link to the pathway, not to the speed of the impulse itself.

exam.q: Explain why reflexes are important to the body.
model: They are rapid / automatic responses.
So they protect the body from harm / reduce damage (e.g. less of a burn).
exam.tip: State the feature, then the benefit.

exam.q: Describe how the signal passes from the sensory neurone to the relay neurone in a reflex arc.
model: A neurotransmitter is released from the end of the sensory neurone.
It diffuses across the synapse / gap.
It binds to receptors on the relay neurone and generates a new impulse.
exam.tip: The impulse itself does not cross the gap.

exam.q: Explain how the structure of a reflex arc allows a person to pull their hand away quickly from a sharp object.
model: Receptors in the skin detect the stimulus and generate an impulse.
A sensory neurone carries the impulse to the spinal cord / CNS.
A relay neurone passes it directly to a motor neurone, so the conscious part of the brain is not involved / there are few synapses.
The motor neurone carries the impulse to the muscle (effector), which contracts.
exam.tip: Name every structure in order and include the reason it is quick.

exam.q: A bright light is shone into a person's eye and the pupil becomes smaller. Describe the pathway taken by the impulses in this reflex and explain why the response is useful.
model: Receptor cells in the retina detect the (bright) light.
Impulses travel along a sensory neurone to the CNS / brain.
The signal passes across a synapse to a relay neurone, and then across another synapse to a motor neurone.
The motor neurone carries impulses to the effector, the muscles of the iris.
The muscles contract and the pupil gets smaller, so less light enters the eye.
This protects the retina / receptor cells from damage by bright light; the response is automatic and rapid.
exam.tip: For 6 marks: correct order, correct names, and a clear benefit linked to this example.

exam.q: The total length of the neurones in a reflex arc is 1.4 m. Impulses travel at 70 m/s. Calculate the time taken for an impulse to travel along the neurones.
model: time = distance / speed = 1.4 / 70
exam.tip: Rearrange speed = distance / time before substituting.

worked.q: In a withdrawal reflex the impulse travels 0.75 m along a sensory neurone and 0.75 m along a motor neurone, both at 75 m/s. There are two synapses, each causing a delay of 0.5 ms. Calculate the total time for the signal to travel round the arc, in ms.
steps: Total distance along neurones = 0.75 + 0.75 = 1.5 m (the relay neurone is so short it is ignored).
Time along neurones = distance / speed = 1.5 / 75 = 0.02 s.
Convert to ms: 0.02 x 1000 = 20 ms.
Delay at synapses = 2 x 0.5 = 1 ms.
Total time = 20 + 1 = 21 ms.
worked.ans: 21 ms

worked.q: A doctor taps just below a patient's kneecap and the lower leg kicks forward. Describe the reflex arc involved.
steps: Identify the stimulus: the tap, which stretches the thigh muscle.
Receptors detect the stimulus and generate electrical impulses.
A sensory neurone carries the impulses to the spinal cord.
In the spinal cord the signal is passed across synapses to a motor neurone. (In the general model you are expected to use, this is by way of a relay neurone.)
The motor neurone carries impulses to the effector, the thigh muscle.
The muscle contracts, so the lower leg kicks forward: this is the response.
worked.ans: tap (stimulus) -> receptor -> sensory neurone -> spinal cord (relay neurone) -> motor neurone -> thigh muscle (effector) contracts -> leg kicks forward

worked.q: A student says: 'I felt the pin prick, so I decided to move my finger.' Use your knowledge of the reflex arc to explain why this is wrong.
steps: The movement is a reflex: receptors in the skin generate impulses that travel along a sensory neurone to the spinal cord.
A relay neurone passes the signal straight to a motor neurone, which carries impulses to the arm muscle, so the finger moves without any decision being made.
Impulses are also sent up the spinal cord to the brain, but this route is longer and has more synapses.
So the conscious part of the brain receives the information after the response has already begun: the feeling of pain comes after the movement, it does not cause it.
worked.ans: The finger moved automatically because of the reflex arc through the spinal cord; awareness of the pain arrived at the conscious brain slightly later by a separate, slower route.

The dashed route up to the conscious part of the brain and back is longer and has more synapses, so it is not used to produce the reflex response.

bio_edx.1.2.summary: Cancer is the result of **changes in cells that lead to uncontrolled cell division**. Normally, mitosis is tightly controlled so that new cells are only made when they are needed for growth or repair. If the genes that control division are changed (mutated), a cell can divide again and again by mitosis without stopping, producing a mass of cells called a **tumour**. This note explains what goes wrong, why it matters and how to word answers for Edexcel.

core.h: The spec statement in one line
core.p: Edexcel asks you to **describe cancer as the result of changes in cells that lead to uncontrolled cell division**. Every answer on this point is built from three ideas: a **change** in the cell, loss of **control**, and **cell division** (mitosis) that does not stop.
bullets: Cancer is not caught like a cold: it begins with a change inside one of the body's own cells.
The change affects how the cell controls division.
The cell then divides by **mitosis** over and over again.
The result is a growing mass of cells called a **tumour**.
The key phrase to learn is **uncontrolled cell division**.

callouts.p: A disease that is the result of changes in cells that lead to uncontrolled cell division.
'Uncontrolled cell division' (or 'cells divide uncontrollably'). Rapid or fast division on its own is usually not enough.

core.h: How cell division is normally controlled
core.p: To understand cancer you first need the normal situation. Body cells divide by mitosis for growth and for repair. They do not divide all the time: division is switched on when new cells are needed and switched off when there are enough.
bullets: The instructions that control when a cell divides are carried by **genes** in the cell's DNA.
Some cells, such as skin cells, divide often because cells are constantly lost and need replacing.
Other cells divide rarely or not at all once they are fully formed.
When a cut has healed, the cells around it stop dividing, because enough new cells have been made.
Because of this control, the number of cells made roughly matches the number of cells needed, so tissues and organs keep their correct size and shape.

callouts.t: Control means stopping as well as starting
callouts.p: Healthy cells respond to signals that tell them to stop dividing. Cancer cells do not.

core.p: The 'changes in cells' in the spec statement are changes in the cell's **DNA**. A change in DNA is called a **mutation**. If a mutation happens in a gene that controls cell division, the control can be lost.
bullets: Mutations happen by chance when DNA is copied before a cell divides.
Most mutations have no effect on the cell at all.
A mutation matters for cancer only if it affects genes that control when the cell divides.

Usually several changes need to build up in the same cell before control is lost completely. This is one reason why cancer is more common in older people: there has been more time for changes to build up.
When the changed cell divides by mitosis, both daughter cells inherit the same change, because mitosis produces genetically identical cells.

callouts.p: A change in the DNA (genetic material) of a cell.
Do not write 'mutations cause cancer' as if all of them do. Say that changes in the genes that control cell division can lead to uncontrolled cell division.

core.h: From one changed cell to a tumour
core.p: Once control is lost, the cell keeps dividing by mitosis. Its daughter cells carry the same change, so they keep dividing too. The number of cells rises faster and faster, and the extra cells pile up as a lump.
bullets: Step 1: a change (mutation) happens in the DNA of one cell.
Step 2: the cell no longer controls its division.
Step 3: the cell divides by mitosis when it should not, and does not stop.
Step 4: all the daughter cells also divide uncontrollably, because they are genetically identical to the changed cell.
Step 5: a mass of cells, a **tumour**, forms.
The tumour can press on or damage the surrounding tissue, so the organ cannot work properly.

callouts.p: A mass (lump) of cells produced by uncontrolled cell division.
The division in cancer is **mitosis**. A 3 mark answer often has a mark for naming it.

core.h: Normal cells compared with cancer cells
core.p: A comparison table is a quick way to revise the differences. An exam question may show a photograph or diagram of both and ask you to describe what is different.
bullets: Both types of cell divide by mitosis. The difference is control.
Cancer cells use a lot of energy and nutrients because they are dividing so often.
Cancer cells do not usually carry out the normal function of the tissue.

head: Feature
Normal cells
Cancer cells
rows: Only when new cells are needed
Repeatedly, even when no new cells are needed
Yes, when enough cells have been made
Tissue of the correct size and shape

core.p: A lump of extra cells may sound harmless, but it can stop organs doing their jobs.
bullets: The tumour takes up space and can **press on** or block nearby structures such as blood vessels, airways or parts of the gut.
Tumour cells use glucose, oxygen and other nutrients that healthy cells need.
Healthy tissue can be damaged or replaced by cells that do not do the tissue's normal job.
The effect depends on where the tumour is: a tumour in the lung reduces the area available for gas exchange; a tumour in the brain can press on areas that control body functions.

callouts.p: In 'explain' questions, say what the tumour does (for example blocks an airway) and what that leads to (less air reaches the alveoli).

core.p: The Edexcel statement only requires cancer as uncontrolled cell division, but exam contexts often mention tumours spreading, so it is worth understanding. Doctors describe tumours as benign or malignant.
bullets: A **benign** tumour grows in one place and does not spread to other parts of the body. It is not cancer, although it can still cause harm by pressing on organs.
A **malignant** tumour is cancer. Its cells can invade neighbouring tissue.
Cells can break off a malignant tumour and be carried in the **blood** to other parts of the body.
There they carry on dividing and form new tumours called **secondary tumours**.
This is why finding and treating cancer early gives a better chance of success: there has been less time for it to spread.

callouts.t: If the question gives you these words
callouts.p: Use them. If it does not, 'uncontrolled cell division forming a tumour' is what Edexcel is looking for.

core.h: What makes the changes more likely
core.p: Changes in DNA can happen by chance, but some things make them more likely. Anything that increases the chance of developing a disease is called a **risk factor**. A substance or agent that causes cancer is called a **carcinogen**.
bullets: **Chemicals in tobacco smoke** (in the tar) damage DNA in cells lining the lungs and airways, increasing the risk of lung cancer.
**Ultraviolet (UV) radiation** from the Sun or sunbeds damages DNA in skin cells, increasing the risk of skin cancer.
**Ionising radiation** such as X-rays and gamma rays can damage DNA.
Some people **inherit** alleles that make certain cancers more likely.
A risk factor raises the probability of cancer. It does not mean a person will definitely get it, and people with no known risk factors can still develop cancer.

callouts.p: A substance or agent that causes cancer by damaging DNA.
Write 'increases the risk of' rather than 'causes' when describing data about lifestyle and cancer.

core.h: Cancer and the rate of mitosis
core.p: Because cancer cells divide so often, a sample of cancer tissue viewed under a microscope shows a higher proportion of cells in mitosis than normal tissue. Exam questions use this in calculations.
bullets: Count the cells that can be seen dividing and the total number of cells in the field of view.
Percentage of cells dividing = (number of cells in mitosis / total number of cells) x 100.
A higher percentage than in normal tissue of the same type suggests that division is not being controlled.
Doubling questions also appear: each round of division doubles the number of cells, so the number after n divisions from one cell is 2^n.

head: Number of divisions
Number of cells from one cancer cell

callouts.t: Why tumours seem to appear suddenly
callouts.p: Doubling means growth speeds up. Twenty rounds of division turn one cell into over a million cells.

core.h: Why cancer treatments target dividing cells
core.p: You do not need details of treatments for this point, but the idea is a useful application of 'uncontrolled cell division' and appears in exam contexts.
bullets: Tumours can sometimes be removed by surgery.
Radiotherapy and chemotherapy damage or kill cells that are dividing.
Because cancer cells divide much more often than most normal cells, they are affected most.
Normal cells that also divide often, such as those making hair, are affected too, which explains some side effects such as hair loss.

callouts.p: If a question describes a drug that 'stops mitosis', explain that the tumour cells can no longer divide, so the tumour stops growing.

core.p: Most questions on this point are worth 1 to 3 marks. Longer ones give you a context or data to interpret.
bullets: Start with the cause: a **change (mutation) in the DNA or genes** of a cell.
State the consequence: **uncontrolled cell division** by **mitosis**.
State the result: a **tumour** forms.
If asked about harm, say what the tumour does to the surrounding tissue or organ.
If given data, quote numbers from it and describe the trend before explaining it.

callouts.p: Individual cells do not grow huge. They **divide** uncontrollably, so the number of cells increases.

analogy.t: A photocopier with a jammed start button
analogy.p: A normal cell is like a photocopier that makes a copy only when someone presses the button and stops when the right number has been made. A cancer cell is like a photocopier whose start button has jammed down: it churns out copy after copy that nobody asked for, and every copy it makes has the same jammed button and starts copying too. Paper piles up in a heap (the tumour) and gets in the way of the rest of the office. Where it breaks down: a jammed button is a single fault you can see and fix, whereas cancer usually needs several changes in DNA to build up, and the copies are living cells that use up the body's food and oxygen and can move to other places.

terms.d: A disease that is the result of changes in cells that lead to uncontrolled cell division.
Cells dividing repeatedly by mitosis when new cells are not needed, and not stopping.
Cell division that produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells; the type of division that is uncontrolled in cancer.
A mass (lump) of cells produced by uncontrolled cell division.
A change in the DNA of a cell.
A section of DNA that codes for a protein; some genes control when a cell divides.
The molecule that carries the genetic information of a cell.
A tumour that stays in one place and does not spread to other tissues; it is not cancer.
A cancerous tumour whose cells can invade nearby tissue and spread to other parts of the body.
A new tumour formed when cancer cells are carried in the blood to another part of the body and divide there.
A substance or agent that causes cancer by damaging DNA, for example chemicals in tobacco smoke.
Something that increases the chance of developing a disease.
The two cells produced when a cell divides by mitosis.
Radiation from the Sun and sunbeds that can damage DNA in skin cells.

mistakes.w: Cancer is when cells grow uncontrollably.
mistakes.r: Cancer is **uncontrolled cell division**: the number of cells increases because cells keep dividing.

mistakes.w: Cancer cells divide by meiosis.
mistakes.r: Cancer cells divide by **mitosis**.

mistakes.w: Cancer is caused by cells dividing quickly.
mistakes.r: The key idea is **loss of control**: the cells divide when they are not needed and do not stop.

mistakes.w: All mutations cause cancer.
mistakes.r: Only changes that affect the genes controlling cell division can lead to cancer; most mutations have no effect.

mistakes.w: A tumour is one very large cell.
mistakes.r: A tumour is a **mass of many cells** produced by repeated division.

mistakes.w: Smoking gives you cancer.
mistakes.r: Smoking **increases the risk** of cancer because chemicals in the smoke damage DNA; it does not make cancer certain.

mistakes.w: You can catch cancer from someone who has it.
mistakes.r: Cancer starts from changes in a person's own cells; it is not passed from person to person.

mistakes.w: Cancer cells are a different kind of cell that enters the body.
mistakes.r: Cancer cells are the body's own cells in which the control of division has been changed.

exam.q: State what is meant by the term cancer.
model: Uncontrolled cell division
exam.tip: Three words get the mark. 'Uncontrolled growth of cells' is weaker.

exam.q: Name the type of cell division that is uncontrolled in cancer.
model: Mitosis
exam.tip: Spell it clearly.

exam.q: Describe how a tumour forms.
model: A change / mutation occurs in the DNA (genes) of a cell
The cell divides uncontrollably
by mitosis, producing a mass of cells
exam.tip: Change, uncontrolled, mitosis, mass of cells: any three of these ideas.

exam.q: Give one difference between the division of a normal cell and the division of a cancer cell.
model: Division of a normal cell is controlled / stops when enough cells are made, but division of a cancer cell is uncontrolled / does not stop
exam.tip: A difference needs both sides stated.

exam.q: Explain why all the cells in a tumour divide uncontrollably.
model: The tumour cells are all produced by mitosis from the original changed cell
so they are genetically identical and all carry the same change (mutation)
exam.tip: Link back to the product of mitosis.

exam.q: A tumour is growing in a person's lung. Explain how this could affect the person.
model: The tumour takes up space / blocks airways / damages lung tissue
so less air reaches the alveoli / less gas exchange can take place
exam.tip: State what the tumour does, then the effect on the organ's function.

exam.q: A drug stops cells from carrying out mitosis. Explain why this drug could be used to treat cancer.
model: Cancer is caused by uncontrolled cell division / cancer cells divide by mitosis
If mitosis is stopped, the tumour cells cannot divide so the tumour stops growing
exam.tip: Apply the definition to the unfamiliar context.

exam.q: Explain why exposure to ultraviolet radiation increases the risk of skin cancer.
model: Ultraviolet radiation damages / changes the DNA in skin cells (causes mutations)
which can lead to uncontrolled cell division
exam.tip: Say 'increases the risk' and finish with the spec phrase.

exam.q: A scientist looks at 400 cells from a tumour and finds that 60 are dividing. In normal tissue of the same type, 12 out of 400 cells are dividing. Calculate the percentage of dividing cells in each sample and explain the difference.
model: Normal tissue: (12 / 400) x 100 = 3%
A higher percentage of the tumour cells are dividing
because division in cancer cells is uncontrolled / they divide when new cells are not needed
exam.tip: Show the working for both calculations, then compare, then explain.

exam.q: Explain how a change in one cell can lead to the development of a tumour that damages an organ.
model: Normally cell division is controlled so that cells only divide when new cells are needed
A change (mutation) occurs in the DNA of a cell, in genes that control cell division
The cell loses control of division and divides repeatedly by mitosis
Mitosis produces genetically identical cells, so all the daughter cells carry the same change and also divide uncontrollably
The number of cells doubles with each division, forming a mass of cells called a tumour
The tumour takes up space, presses on or damages surrounding tissue and uses nutrients needed by healthy cells
so the organ cannot carry out its function properly
exam.tip: Write it as a logical sequence: normal control, change, uncontrolled mitosis, tumour, effect.

worked.q: One cancer cell divides by mitosis every 3 days. Assuming every cell keeps dividing and none die, how many cells are there after 30 days?
steps: Number of divisions = 30 / 3 = 10.
Each division doubles the number of cells, so number of cells = 2^10.
worked.ans: 1024 cells

worked.q: In a sample of tissue, 27 out of 450 cells are in mitosis. Calculate the percentage of cells in mitosis.
steps: Write the fraction: 27 / 450.
Multiply by 100 to convert to a percentage: 0.06 x 100 = 6.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why a person who smokes has a higher risk of developing lung cancer than a non-smoker. (3 marks)
steps: Identify the cause: tobacco smoke contains chemicals that are carcinogens.
Say what they do: these chemicals damage (change) the DNA in cells lining the lungs.
Link to the definition of cancer: if the genes that control cell division are changed, the cells divide uncontrollably by mitosis and form a tumour.
Use careful language: this increases the risk; it does not mean every smoker will get lung cancer.
worked.ans: Carcinogens in smoke change the DNA of lung cells, which can lead to uncontrolled cell division and a tumour, so the risk is higher.
