callouts.p: I Prefer My Apples Totally Crunchy: Interphase, Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase, Cytokinesis.

core.h: Why the daughter cells are genetically identical
core.p: Mitosis produces **two genetically identical daughter cells** because of two things working together. First, in interphase **DNA replication copies every chromosome exactly**, making two identical sister chromatids. Second, in anaphase **one chromatid of every chromosome goes to each pole**. So each new nucleus gets one complete, identical copy of all the DNA in the parent cell.
bullets: Exact copying of DNA means the **alleles (gene versions)** are the same in both copies.
Separating **sister chromatids** (which are identical) rather than pairs keeps all the genetic information in both cells.
No mixing or shuffling of genes happens in mitosis, so there is **no genetic variation** (unlike meiosis and fertilisation).
Rare **mutations** (copying errors) during replication are the only way daughter cells can differ.

callouts.p: DNA is replicated (copied) before division AND sister chromatids are separated equally so each cell receives one copy of each chromosome.

core.h: Why the daughter cells are diploid
core.p: Each daughter cell is **diploid**, with the **same number of chromosomes as the parent**. A human body cell with 46 chromosomes divides by mitosis to make two cells with 46 chromosomes each. The chromosome number is kept the same because the DNA is **doubled** in interphase and then **halved** between the two cells, so it ends up where it started.
bullets: 46 chromosomes (1 chromatid each) to 46 chromosomes (2 chromatids each) after replication.
Mitosis shares these out: 46 chromatids go to each pole, giving 46 chromosomes in each new cell.
Keeping the number constant means every body cell has a **full set of genes** and can work properly.
If chromosome number changed each division, cells would soon lose genes or have too many copies, which could stop them working.

head: Feature
Mitosis
Meiosis (for comparison)
rows: Yes, to each other and the parent
Body cells for growth, repair, asexual reproduction

core.p: You can see mitosis in a light microscope by looking at the **tip of a plant root** (for example an onion or garlic root), where cells are dividing quickly in the **meristem**. The tip is softened in acid, **stained** so chromosomes show up, squashed into a thin layer and viewed at high power. You can then count how many cells are at each stage.
bullets: Use the **root tip** because cells there are actively dividing; cells further back are elongating, not dividing.
**Hydrochloric acid** breaks down the material holding cells together so they spread out into a single layer.
A **stain** (e.g. toluidine blue or acetic orcein) binds to DNA so chromosomes are visible.
**Squashing** spreads the cells so light passes through one layer of cells.
Most cells seen are in **interphase**, because that is the longest stage.
The proportion of cells in a stage is proportional to **how long that stage lasts**.

callouts.p: Time in a stage = (number of cells in that stage / total cells counted) x total length of the cell cycle.

core.h: Linking ideas: control and uses of mitosis
core.p: Mitosis is how multicellular organisms make new body cells. This point is about **how** it happens; other points cover **why** (growth, repair and asexual reproduction, 2.2) and what goes wrong (cancer, 2.4). Knowing the cycle well helps with both.
bullets: Because daughter cells are identical, tissues made by mitosis are made of cells with the **same genes**, so a cut heals with the same kind of cells.
**Asexual reproduction** by mitosis makes **clones**: offspring genetically identical to the parent.
The cell cycle is controlled by genes; a **mutation** in these genes can cause cells to divide **uncontrollably**, forming a tumour.
Many cancer drugs work by stopping a stage of the cycle (for example by blocking spindle fibres so chromosomes cannot be separated).

analogy.t: Photocopying a recipe book for two kitchens
analogy.p: Imagine a chef has one recipe book (the DNA) and needs to open a second identical kitchen. In interphase she **photocopies every page** (DNA replication) and buys extra pots and pans (organelles). In prophase she **binds each copied page together with its original** so nothing gets lost (chromosomes condense as two chromatids). In metaphase she **lays every pair out in one row** down the middle of the table. In anaphase two assistants **pull each pair apart, one copy to each end** of the table. In telophase each pile is **put into a new folder** (new nuclear membrane). In cytokinesis a wall is built and there are **two kitchens, each with a complete identical book**. Where it breaks down: a photocopier can be careless, but DNA replication is extremely accurate; and a real kitchen does not shrink, whereas each daughter cell starts smaller and must grow before it divides again.

terms.d: The series of stages a cell goes through to divide: interphase, mitosis (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase) and cytokinesis.
Cell division that produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells; the division of the nucleus in the cell cycle.
The longest stage of the cell cycle, in which the cell grows, makes more organelles such as mitochondria and ribosomes, and replicates its DNA.
Copying of DNA so that each chromosome becomes two identical sister chromatids.
A long molecule of DNA, packaged with proteins, that carries many genes; found in the nucleus.
One of two identical copies of a chromosome made by DNA replication, joined to the other at a centromere.
The region where two sister chromatids are joined and where spindle fibres attach.
Protein fibres that form during prophase, attach to centromeres and pull chromatids to opposite poles of the cell.
Stage of mitosis in which chromosomes condense and become visible, the nuclear membrane breaks down and spindle fibres form.
Stage of mitosis in which chromosomes line up along the equator (middle) of the cell, attached to spindle fibres.
Stage of mitosis in which spindle fibres shorten and pull sister chromatids apart to opposite poles.
Stage of mitosis in which a nuclear membrane re-forms around each set of chromosomes, forming two nuclei.
Division of the cytoplasm and cell membrane to form two separate daughter cells.
Having two sets of chromosomes, one from each parent (46 chromosomes in a human body cell).
Having one set of chromosomes (23 in a human gamete); not produced by mitosis.
Having exactly the same DNA, so the same genes and alleles.
The new cells produced when a parent cell divides.

mistakes.w: DNA is copied during prophase.
mistakes.r: DNA replicates during interphase, before mitosis starts; in prophase the already-copied chromosomes condense.

mistakes.w: Interphase is a resting stage where nothing happens.
mistakes.r: Interphase is very active: the cell grows, increases its organelles (mitochondria, ribosomes) and replicates its DNA.

mistakes.w: Mitosis makes four cells.
mistakes.r: Mitosis (with cytokinesis) makes two daughter cells; four cells are made by meiosis.

mistakes.w: The daughter cells are haploid / have half the chromosomes.
mistakes.r: Daughter cells are diploid with the same number of chromosomes as the parent (46 in humans).

mistakes.w: In anaphase the chromosome pairs separate.
mistakes.r: In anaphase the sister chromatids of each chromosome are pulled to opposite poles by spindle fibres.

mistakes.w: Chromosomes line up at the edge of the cell in metaphase.
mistakes.r: Chromosomes line up along the equator / middle of the cell.

mistakes.w: Cytokinesis is the fifth stage of mitosis.
mistakes.r: Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm and cell membrane that follows mitosis; mitosis has four stages.

mistakes.w: Daughter cells are similar to the parent.
mistakes.r: Daughter cells are genetically identical to each other and to the parent cell.

mistakes.w: The cell wall divides in telophase.
mistakes.r: In telophase the nuclear membranes re-form; the cytoplasm and membrane (and in plants, a new cell wall) divide in cytokinesis.

exam.q: Name the stage of the cell cycle in which DNA is replicated.
model: Interphase.
exam.tip: Not prophase and not 'mitosis'.

exam.q: State two things, other than DNA replication, that happen to a cell during interphase.
model: The cell grows / gets bigger.
The number of sub-cellular structures / organelles (e.g. mitochondria, ribosomes) increases.
exam.tip: Name specific organelles to be safe.

exam.q: Give the stage of mitosis in which the chromosomes line up along the middle of the cell.
model: Metaphase.
exam.tip: Middle = Metaphase.

exam.q: Describe what happens during anaphase.
model: Spindle fibres shorten / contract.
Sister chromatids are pulled / separated to opposite poles / ends of the cell.
exam.tip: Use the words chromatids and opposite poles.

exam.q: What is cytokinesis?
model: Division of the cytoplasm and cell membrane to form two (daughter) cells.
exam.tip: Mention cytoplasm; 'cell splits' alone may not score.

exam.q: A human skin cell has 46 chromosomes. State the number of chromosomes in each daughter cell produced by mitosis and explain your answer.
model: DNA/chromosomes are replicated before division and one copy (chromatid) of each chromosome goes into each daughter cell.
exam.tip: A number alone gets 1 mark; the explanation gets the second.

exam.q: Explain why the daughter cells produced by mitosis are genetically identical.
model: DNA is copied exactly (replicated) during interphase, so sister chromatids are identical.
Sister chromatids are separated so each daughter cell receives one copy of every chromosome.
exam.tip: Two separate ideas: copying, then equal sharing.

exam.q: Describe the changes in the nucleus during prophase.
model: Chromosomes condense / coil / become shorter and thicker.
Chromosomes become visible (as two chromatids).
The nuclear membrane breaks down.
(Spindle fibres form.)
exam.tip: Any three; spindle fibres form in the cell rather than the nucleus but are usually credited.

exam.q: Explain why most cells seen in a stained root tip squash are in interphase.
model: Interphase is the longest stage of the cell cycle.
So at any moment more cells are found in interphase than any other stage.
exam.tip: Link the count to the time spent in each stage.

exam.q: Describe the events of the cell cycle that produce two genetically identical diploid cells from one parent cell.
model: In interphase the cell grows and increases its number of organelles such as mitochondria and ribosomes.
DNA replicates so each chromosome is made of two identical sister chromatids.
Prophase: chromosomes condense and become visible; nuclear membrane breaks down; spindle fibres form.
Metaphase: chromosomes line up along the equator, attached to spindle fibres at the centromere.
Anaphase: spindle fibres shorten and pull sister chromatids to opposite poles.
Telophase: nuclear membranes re-form around each set of chromosomes, giving two nuclei.
Cytokinesis: cytoplasm and cell membrane divide to form two cells.
Each cell has the same number of chromosomes as the parent (diploid, 46 in humans) and identical DNA.
exam.tip: Go in order, name every stage and say what the chromosomes do in each. End by linking to identical and diploid.

exam.q: A cell cycle lasts 20 hours. In a sample of 200 cells, 10 were in metaphase. Calculate how long metaphase lasts in minutes.
model: Fraction in metaphase = 10 / 200 = 0.05.
Time = 0.05 x 20 hours = 1 hour.
= 60 minutes.
exam.tip: Watch for a unit change at the end.

worked.q: In a root tip squash, a student counted 400 cells: 340 in interphase, 30 in prophase, 12 in metaphase, 8 in anaphase and 10 in telophase. The cell cycle lasts 24 hours. Calculate how long prophase lasts, in minutes.
steps: Fraction of cells in prophase = 30 / 400 = 0.075.
Assume the fraction of cells in a stage equals the fraction of the cycle spent in that stage.
Time in prophase = 0.075 x 24 hours = 1.8 hours.
Convert to minutes: 1.8 x 60 = 108 minutes.
worked.ans: Prophase lasts about 108 minutes (1.8 hours).

worked.q: A plant cell has 16 chromosomes at the start of interphase. State the number of chromosomes and chromatids in the cell (a) at metaphase and (b) in each daughter cell after cytokinesis.
steps: In interphase every chromosome is replicated, so each of the 16 chromosomes becomes 2 sister chromatids.
(a) At metaphase there are still 16 chromosomes (count the centromeres), but 16 x 2 = 32 chromatids.
In anaphase sister chromatids are separated, one to each pole, so each pole receives 16.
(b) Each daughter cell has 16 chromosomes, each made of one chromatid, so 16 chromatids.
worked.ans: (a) 16 chromosomes, 32 chromatids. (b) 16 chromosomes and 16 chromatids in each daughter cell: diploid, the same as the parent.

worked.q: A diagram shows a cell in which X-shaped chromosomes are arranged in a single line across the centre, with fibres attached from each end of the cell. Name the stage and describe what happens next.
steps: Chromosomes in a single line across the centre, attached to spindle fibres, means metaphase.
The next stage is anaphase.
In anaphase the spindle fibres shorten and the centromeres split.
Sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles of the cell.
worked.ans: Metaphase. Next, in anaphase, spindle fibres shorten and pull the sister chromatids apart to opposite poles.

bio_edx.1.11.summary: The **eye** is a **sense organ** containing **receptor cells** that detect **light** (a stimulus) and convert it into **electrical impulses** that travel along the **optic nerve** to the brain. The **cornea** and **lens** refract (bend) light to focus a clear image on the **retina**; the **iris** controls the size of the **pupil** and so how much light enters; and the retina contains two kinds of receptor cell: **rods**, which work in dim light but do not detect colour, and **cones**, which detect colour in bright light. Knowing each part's structure and how it fits its function is the key to this spec point.

core.h: The eye as a sensory receptor
core.p: A **receptor** is a cell (or group of cells) that detects a **stimulus**, a change in the environment. The eye is a **sense organ**: its receptor cells are in the **retina** and they detect **light**. They convert light energy into **electrical impulses**, which travel along **sensory neurones** in the **optic nerve** to the **brain**, which interprets them as an image.
bullets: Stimulus: **light**.
Receptors: **rod and cone cells** in the **retina**.
Impulses travel along the **optic nerve** (made of sensory neurones) to the brain.
The other parts of the eye exist to **control how much light enters** and to **focus it** on the retina so a clear image forms.
The image formed on the retina is **upside down (inverted)**; the brain interprets it the right way up.

callouts.p: A cell that detects a **stimulus** and converts it into an **electrical impulse**. In the eye, rods and cones in the retina are receptors for light.

core.h: Structure of the eye: the parts and their jobs
core.p: Learn the position of each structure on a diagram and one clear function for each. The Edexcel specification focuses on the **cornea, lens, iris and the rod and cone cells of the retina**, but the other parts help you explain how they work.
bullets: Light passes through the eye in this order: **cornea, pupil (through the iris), lens, retina**.
The **sclera** is the tough white outer coat that protects the eye and keeps its shape.
The **ciliary muscles** and **suspensory ligaments** hold the lens and change its shape.
The **fovea** is the part of the retina directly behind the lens where cones are most densely packed, giving the sharpest colour vision.
The **blind spot** is where the optic nerve leaves the eye; there are **no rods or cones** there, so no light is detected.

head: Structure
Function
rows: Transparent front layer; refracts (bends) light into the eye; does most of the focusing
Coloured ring of muscle; controls the size of the pupil and so how much light enters
Hole in the centre of the iris through which light enters
Transparent, flexible; refracts light to fine-tune the focus on the retina
Contract or relax to change the shape of the lens
Connect the ciliary muscles to the lens
Layer at the back containing light receptor cells (rods and cones)
Area of retina with most cones; sharpest, colour vision
Carries impulses from the retina to the brain
Where the optic nerve leaves the retina; no receptors
Tough white outer layer; protects the eye

core.p: The **cornea** is the **transparent**, curved layer at the very front of the eye. It is curved and light slows down as it enters it, so it **refracts (bends) light** towards the centre of the eye. The cornea does **most of the refraction** needed to focus light on the retina.
bullets: **Transparent** so light can pass through.
**Curved (convex)** so light is bent inwards, towards the lens and retina.
It has **no blood vessels**, which keeps it clear; it gets oxygen from the air and nutrients from the fluid behind it.
Its shape is **fixed**, so it cannot adjust the focus; that is the lens's job.
If the cornea's curvature is wrong, vision is blurred, which is why some sight problems can be corrected by surgery that reshapes the cornea.

callouts.p: The **cornea** does **most** of the refracting but its shape is fixed. The **lens** does less refracting but can **change shape** to fine-tune the focus.

core.p: The **lens** is a transparent, **flexible**, biconvex structure behind the iris. It **refracts light** further so that it is **focused** exactly on the retina. Because it is elastic, its shape can change: this is called **accommodation**, and it lets us focus on both near and distant objects.
bullets: The lens is held in place by **suspensory ligaments**, attached to a ring of **ciliary muscles**.
**Near object**: ciliary muscles **contract**, suspensory ligaments **slacken**, the lens becomes **fatter (more curved)** and refracts light **more strongly**.
**Distant object**: ciliary muscles **relax**, suspensory ligaments are **pulled tight**, the lens is pulled **thinner (less curved)** and refracts light **less**.
Light from near objects is spreading out more, so it needs more bending to be focused on the retina.
If the lens cannot focus light exactly on the retina, the image is **blurred**.

callouts.p: When the ciliary muscles **contract**, the ligaments go **slack**, not tight. Think of the ciliary ring getting smaller, so it pulls less on the lens.

fig.cap: Figure 2: How the eye focuses light. Light rays from an object are refracted most by the curved cornea and then fine-tuned by the lens, so they meet at a point on the retina. The image formed there is inverted and the brain interprets it the right way up.

core.p: The **iris** is the coloured ring of tissue in front of the lens. It contains **muscles** that change the size of the **pupil**, the hole in its centre. This controls **how much light enters the eye**, protecting the retina from damage in bright light and letting in enough light to see in dim conditions.
bullets: The iris contains two sets of muscle: **circular muscles** (in rings around the pupil) and **radial muscles** (running outwards like spokes).
**Bright light**: circular muscles **contract**, radial muscles **relax**, so the pupil becomes **smaller (constricts)**. Less light enters, protecting the **retina** from damage.
**Dim light**: radial muscles **contract**, circular muscles **relax**, so the pupil becomes **larger (dilates)**. More light enters, so more reaches the receptor cells.
This is a **reflex**: it is automatic and rapid, and does not need conscious thought.
The two sets of muscles are **antagonistic**: when one contracts the other relaxes.

callouts.p: Say the pupil **constricts** or gets **smaller**, never that the iris or pupil itself contracts. Muscles contract; pupils change size.

fig.cap: Figure 3: The iris reflex. In bright light the circular muscles of the iris contract and the pupil gets smaller, so less light reaches and damages the retina. In dim light the radial muscles contract and the pupil gets larger, letting more light in.

core.h: The retina: where light is detected
core.p: The **retina** is the light-sensitive layer lining the back of the eye. It contains millions of **receptor cells** of two types, **rods** and **cones**. When light hits them, chemicals (pigments) in the cells change, which triggers **electrical impulses** in sensory neurones. These neurones join to form the **optic nerve**.
bullets: Light energy is converted into **electrical impulses**: this is what makes the retina a receptor.
The retina contains about 120 million rods and about 6 million cones, so **rods far outnumber cones**.
**Cones** are concentrated in the **fovea**, directly opposite the lens; this gives the sharpest, most detailed vision when you look straight at something.
**Rods** are spread across the rest of the retina, especially around the edges, which is why you can see dim objects better out of the corner of your eye.
At the **blind spot** the optic nerve leaves the eye, so there are **no receptor cells** and no image is detected there.

callouts.p: Light, then **rods and cones** in retina, then electrical impulses in **sensory neurones**, then **optic nerve**, then **brain**.

core.p: **Rods** are receptor cells that are **very sensitive to light**, so they work well in **dim light**. They cannot tell different colours apart, so they give **black-and-white (greyscale)** vision.
bullets: Highly sensitive: respond even to **low light intensity**, giving night vision.
Only **one type** of rod, so they cannot distinguish colours.
Found mainly **around the edge** of the retina, not at the fovea.
Many rods connect to the same neurone, which increases sensitivity but gives a **less detailed** image.
This is why in a dark room you can see shapes but not colours.

callouts.p: A receptor cell in the retina that is sensitive to **dim light** but does **not detect colour**.

core.p: **Cones** are receptor cells that need **brighter light** to work. They detect **colour** and give **sharp, detailed** vision. There are **three types of cone**, each most sensitive to a different colour of light: **red, green and blue**.
bullets: Need **bright light**, so in very dim light cones do not respond and we lose colour vision.
Three types (red-, green- and blue-sensitive); the brain compares how strongly each type is stimulated to see the full range of colours.
Concentrated at the **fovea**, giving detailed colour vision in the centre of the field of view.
If one type of cone is missing or faulty, the person cannot distinguish some colours, which is **colour blindness** (often red-green).
Each cone tends to connect to its own neurone, which gives **high detail (sharp images)**.

head: Feature
Rods
Cones
rows: Yes, three types: red, green, blue
Around the edge of the retina

callouts.p: A receptor cell in the retina that works in **bright light** and detects **colour**; there are three types, sensitive to **red, green and blue** light.

fig.cap: Figure 4: Receptor cells in the retina. Rods are long and thin and respond to dim light but not colour. Cones are shorter and come in three types sensitive to red, green and blue light; they need bright light. Both trigger impulses in neurones that form the optic nerve.

core.h: How the eye adapts to light and dark
core.p: Two systems work together when light levels change: the **iris** changes pupil size quickly, and the balance between **rods and cones** shifts more slowly.
bullets: Walking into a dark room: at first you see very little; the pupils **dilate** at once, and over the next minutes the **rods** become more sensitive, so you gradually see shapes in black and white.
Walking into bright sunlight: the pupils **constrict** quickly to protect the retina, and the **cones** take over, giving colour vision.
Colours seem to disappear at dusk because there is not enough light for the cones, so only rods are working.
Faint stars are easier to see when you look slightly to one side of them, because the light then falls on rod-rich areas of the retina instead of the cone-rich fovea.

callouts.p: Questions often describe a situation (night driving, a cat's eyes, a cinema) and ask you to explain it using rods, cones and the iris. Always name the cell or muscle and say what it does.

core.p: Higher-grade answers link each structure to a feature that suits its function.
bullets: **Cornea**: transparent and curved, to let light in and refract it.
**Lens**: transparent, elastic and biconvex, so it refracts light and can change shape for near and far focusing.
**Iris**: contains antagonistic circular and radial muscles, to control pupil size quickly by reflex.
**Retina**: packed with millions of receptor cells; cones concentrated at the fovea for detail; rods spread widely for sensitivity.
**Optic nerve**: bundle of sensory neurones, carrying impulses rapidly to the brain.
**Sclera**: tough, to protect the delicate inner structures and keep the eyeball's shape.

core.h: Linking the eye to the nervous system
core.p: The eye is the start of a sensory pathway. The information it collects only becomes vision when the brain processes it.
bullets: **Stimulus** (light) is detected by **receptors** (rods and cones).
Impulses pass along **sensory neurones** in the optic nerve to the brain.
An area at the **back of the cerebrum** processes visual information and interprets the image.
The **pupil reflex** shows the eye also acting as part of a reflex arc: impulses from the retina trigger a rapid automatic response by the iris muscles (effectors).
Damage to the retina, optic nerve or visual areas of the brain can all cause loss of vision.

callouts.p: In the pupil reflex the **muscles of the iris** are the **effectors**: they respond to impulses by contracting.

core.p: Questions range from labelling a diagram (1 mark each) to explaining how the eye responds to changes in light or distance (4 to 6 marks).
bullets: For labels, practise drawing and labelling the eye from memory: cornea, iris, pupil, lens, ciliary muscle, suspensory ligament, retina, fovea, optic nerve, blind spot.
For functions, use precise verbs: the cornea **refracts**, the lens **focuses / refracts**, the iris **controls pupil size**, the retina **contains receptors**, the optic nerve **carries impulses**.
For rods vs cones, always give a comparison: rods work in **dim light** but **not colour**; cones work in **bright light** and **detect colour**.
For the iris, name **which muscles contract** and the **effect** on pupil size and light entering.
Describe impulses as **electrical impulses**, not messages or signals of light.

callouts.p: Light is **refracted**, not reflected, by the cornea and lens. The retina **detects** light; it does not focus it. The optic nerve carries **impulses**, not light or images.

analogy.t: The eye as a digital camera
analogy.p: The eye works like a **digital camera**. The **cornea** is the fixed front glass that does most of the bending of light; the **lens** is the adjustable focus ring; the **iris** is the aperture that opens wider in dim light and closes down in bright light; the **retina** is the image sensor, with **rods** like a high-sensitivity black-and-white night mode and **cones** like red, green and blue colour pixels; and the **optic nerve** is the cable that carries the data to the computer (the brain), which processes the picture. Where it breaks down: a camera focuses by moving the lens backwards and forwards, but the eye focuses by **changing the shape** of the lens; a camera sensor has the same pixels everywhere, whereas the retina has cones packed in the fovea and rods around the edges; and the image is not stored in the eye but interpreted by the brain.

terms.d: An organ containing receptor cells that detect a particular stimulus; the eye detects light.
A cell that detects a stimulus and converts it into an electrical impulse.
A change in the environment that can be detected, such as a change in light intensity.
Transparent, curved front layer of the eye that refracts light and does most of the focusing.
Transparent, flexible structure that refracts light and changes shape to focus light on the retina.
The bending of light as it passes from one material into another.
Coloured ring of muscle that controls the size of the pupil and so the amount of light entering the eye.
The hole in the centre of the iris through which light enters the eye.
Iris muscles arranged in rings; they contract in bright light to make the pupil smaller.
Iris muscles arranged like spokes; they contract in dim light to make the pupil larger.
Light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye containing rod and cone receptor cells.
Receptor cell sensitive to dim light that does not detect colour.
Receptor cell that works in bright light and detects colour; three types sensitive to red, green and blue light.
Area of the retina with the highest density of cones, giving the sharpest colour vision.
Bundle of sensory neurones carrying electrical impulses from the retina to the brain.
Point where the optic nerve leaves the retina; it has no rods or cones so cannot detect light.
Changing the shape of the lens, using the ciliary muscles and suspensory ligaments, to focus on near or distant objects.

mistakes.w: The lens does all the focusing.
mistakes.r: The cornea does most of the refraction; the lens fine-tunes the focus by changing shape.

mistakes.w: The cornea and lens reflect light onto the retina.
mistakes.r: They refract (bend) light so that it is focused on the retina.

mistakes.w: In bright light the pupil contracts.
mistakes.r: In bright light the circular muscles of the iris contract, so the pupil becomes smaller (constricts).

mistakes.w: Rods detect colour and cones work in the dark.
mistakes.r: Rods are sensitive to dim light but do not detect colour; cones need bright light and detect colour.

mistakes.w: The pupil gets smaller in bright light so we can see better.
mistakes.r: The pupil gets smaller to reduce the light entering and so protect the retina from damage.

mistakes.w: The optic nerve carries light to the brain.
mistakes.r: The optic nerve carries electrical impulses from the receptor cells to the brain.

mistakes.w: The retina focuses the image.
mistakes.r: The retina contains receptor cells that detect light; focusing is done by the cornea and lens.

mistakes.w: When the ciliary muscles contract the suspensory ligaments are pulled tight.
mistakes.r: When the ciliary muscles contract the suspensory ligaments slacken, so the lens becomes fatter for near vision.

mistakes.w: The blind spot has only rods.
mistakes.r: The blind spot has no receptor cells at all, because it is where the optic nerve leaves the eye.

exam.q: Name the part of the eye that contains light receptor cells.
model: Retina
exam.tip: Not the optic nerve, which carries the impulses.

exam.q: State the function of the iris.
model: Controls the size of the pupil / controls how much light enters the eye
exam.tip: Mention the pupil or the amount of light.

exam.q: Give the function of the cornea.
model: Refracts / bends light (into the eye) / focuses light
exam.tip: Use the word refracts.

exam.q: Describe the role of the cornea and the lens in producing a clear image.
model: both refract / bend light
so that light is focused on the retina
(cornea does most refraction; lens changes shape to fine-tune focus)
exam.tip: Say where the light is focused: on the retina.

exam.q: Describe the differences between rod cells and cone cells.
model: rods are sensitive to dim light whereas cones need bright light
cones detect colour whereas rods do not / rods give black and white vision
cones are concentrated in the fovea whereas rods are found around the edge of the retina
there are three types of cone but one type of rod
exam.tip: Each point must compare both cells.

exam.q: Explain why it is difficult to see colours in dim light.
model: cones (which detect colour) need bright light to work
in dim light only rods are stimulated and rods do not detect colour
exam.tip: Two linked points: cones fail, rods cannot see colour.

exam.q: Explain how the iris responds when a person walks from a dark room into bright sunlight.
model: receptors in the retina detect the increase in light
circular muscles of the iris contract
radial muscles relax
pupil becomes smaller / constricts
less light enters the eye, preventing damage to the retina
exam.tip: Name both muscles and say what each does, then the effect.

exam.q: Explain how the eye changes to focus on a nearby object.
model: ciliary muscles contract
suspensory ligaments slacken
lens becomes fatter / more curved and refracts light more
light is focused on the retina
exam.tip: Learn the sequence in order: muscles, ligaments, lens shape, refraction.

exam.q: Suggest why a person cannot see an object whose image falls on the blind spot.
model: the blind spot is where the optic nerve leaves the eye
there are no rods or cones / receptor cells there so no impulses are produced
exam.tip: Link the structure to the lack of receptors.

exam.q: Owls hunt at night. Their retinas contain a very high proportion of rod cells. Explain how this helps them.
model: rods are very sensitive to (dim) light
so owls can see / detect prey in low light at night
exam.tip: Apply what you know about rods to the animal in the question.

exam.q: Describe how the structures of the eye allow it to act as a sensory receptor that detects light and forms an image.
model: light enters through the transparent cornea, which refracts light
the iris controls the size of the pupil to control how much light enters
circular muscles contract in bright light to make the pupil smaller; radial muscles contract in dim light to make it larger
the lens refracts light and changes shape (ciliary muscles, suspensory ligaments) to focus light on the retina
the retina contains receptor cells: rods for dim light, cones for colour in bright light
three types of cone, red, green and blue; cones concentrated at the fovea
receptors convert light into electrical impulses
impulses travel along the optic nerve to the brain
exam.tip: Follow the path of light through the eye and finish with the impulses reaching the brain.

worked.q: A student enters a cinema from a sunny street. At first she cannot see the seats, but after a few minutes she can make out the shapes of people, though not the colours of their clothes. Explain these observations.
steps: In bright sunlight her pupils were small (circular muscles contracted), so little light entered the eye.
In the dark cinema there is very little light, so at first not enough reaches the retina for her to see.
The iris responds by reflex: radial muscles contract and circular muscles relax, so the pupils dilate and more light enters.
Over a few minutes the rods become more sensitive; rods work in dim light, so she can now see shapes.
Rods do not detect colour, and there is not enough light for the cones, so she cannot see colours.
worked.ans: Her pupils dilate and her rod cells, which are sensitive to dim light, gradually allow her to see shapes. Because cones need bright light and rods cannot detect colour, she sees in black and white.

worked.q: A person looks up from a book to a mountain in the distance. Describe and explain the changes in their eye.
steps: Light from the distant mountain needs less refraction to be focused on the retina than light from the near book.
The ciliary muscles relax.
The suspensory ligaments are pulled tight.
The lens is pulled thinner (less curved), so it refracts light less.
Light from the mountain is now focused on the retina, so the image is clear; the cornea's refraction stays the same because its shape is fixed.
worked.ans: The ciliary muscles relax, the suspensory ligaments tighten and the lens becomes thinner, refracting light less so that the image of the distant mountain is focused on the retina.

bio_edx.1.3.summary: Growth is a permanent increase in size or mass. In **animals** growth happens by **cell division (mitosis)** and **cell differentiation**, and most cells lose the ability to differentiate early in life. In **plants** growth happens by **cell division** in the **meristems**, **cell elongation** (cells get longer by taking water into their vacuoles) and **differentiation**, and plants keep the ability to grow and differentiate all their lives. **Differentiation** is the process by which a cell becomes **specialised**: genes are switched on or off so the cell develops the structures it needs for one particular **function**, and specialised cells are grouped into tissues, organs and organ systems.

core.p: **Growth** is a **permanent increase in size, length or mass** of an organism. It is not just swelling up with water for a few hours. Multicellular organisms grow by making **more cells** and by those cells **becoming specialised**; plants can also grow by making cells **longer**.
bullets: Growth can be measured as an increase in **height or length**, **wet (fresh) mass**, **dry mass** or **number of cells**.
**Dry mass** is the most reliable measure because water content can change from hour to hour, but measuring it **kills** the organism.
**Wet mass** and length can be measured without harming the organism, so they are used for humans and for tracking the same plant over time.
Growth rate = increase in size / time taken.
Percentage change = (final value - starting value) / starting value x 100.

callouts.p: A permanent increase in the size or mass of an organism.

core.p: The spec names three processes. **Cell division** makes more cells. **Cell elongation** makes plant cells longer. **Cell differentiation** makes cells specialised. Animals rely on division and differentiation; plants use all three.
bullets: **Cell division** is by **mitosis**, producing genetically identical diploid daughter cells.
**Cell elongation** happens only in **plants**: a cell expands as water enters its **vacuole**.
**Cell differentiation** turns unspecialised cells into **specialised cells** that carry out a particular function.

head: Process
Animals
Plants
rows: Yes, in many tissues; rate falls after childhood
Yes, mainly in meristems at shoot and root tips
Yes, in the zone just behind the meristem

callouts.p: Animals: cell division and differentiation. Plants: cell division, elongation and differentiation.

core.p: In animals, growth happens by **cell division** (mitosis) to increase the number of cells, followed by **differentiation** so the new cells become specialised. Most animal cells **differentiate at an early stage** of development and then **lose the ability to differentiate** into other cell types. Animals usually **stop growing** when they reach adult size, although cell division continues for **repair and replacement** (for example skin and blood cells).
bullets: Growth occurs throughout the body, not in particular growing points.
Specialised animal cells usually keep their type: a muscle cell divides to make muscle cells only.
Adults still have some **adult stem cells** (for example in bone marrow) that can make a limited range of cells (covered in 2.8).
Growth is controlled by **hormones** and genes, and can be monitored using percentile charts (2.7).

callouts.p: Only plant cells grow by elongation. Do not write about elongation for animals.

core.h: Growth in plants: meristems and cell division
core.p: Plant growth starts in **meristems**: regions of unspecialised cells at the **tips of shoots and roots** (and in a ring in the stem for growth in width). Meristem cells divide rapidly by **mitosis**. They stay **unspecialised** and can differentiate into **any type of plant cell** throughout the plant's life.
bullets: Meristem cells are small, with **thin walls**, **large nuclei** and **no large vacuole**.
Root tip meristems are protected by a **root cap**.
Because meristems stay active all the plant's life, plants can **keep growing** and **regrow** lost parts.
This is why gardeners can take **cuttings** and grow a whole new plant from a small piece of stem.

callouts.p: A region of unspecialised, dividing cells in a plant, found at the tips of roots and shoots.

fig.cap: A growing root tip. Cells divide by mitosis in the meristem just behind the root cap, then get longer in the zone of elongation, then differentiate further back (for example into root hair cells). The oldest cells are furthest from the tip.

core.p: Just behind the meristem is the **zone of elongation**. Here new cells **take in water by osmosis** into their **vacuoles**. The vacuole swells and pushes the cell wall outwards, so the cell gets much **longer**. This pushes the root tip down through the soil and the shoot tip up towards the light. Elongation is responsible for most of the **increase in length** of a root or shoot.
bullets: Water moves into the cell by **osmosis**, from a dilute solution outside to the more concentrated cell sap inside.
The **large permanent vacuole** fills with water and the cell becomes **turgid**.
The cell wall stretches and lengthens; new cellulose is added to it.
Elongation adds length **without adding more cells**, which is a cheap way to grow quickly.
(Triple link) The plant hormone **auxin** promotes cell elongation; unequal auxin explains phototropism and gravitropism (Topic 6).

callouts.p: In the zone of elongation the number of cells stays the same; each cell just gets longer.

core.p: **Differentiation** is the process by which an unspecialised cell becomes a **specialised cell** with a particular **structure** suited to a particular **function**. Every body cell has the **same genes**, but in differentiation **some genes are switched on and others switched off**. The genes that are switched on make the proteins that build the structures the cell needs, for example lots of mitochondria, a flagellum or cilia.
bullets: Differentiation changes a cell's **shape**, its **sub-cellular structures** and the **proteins** it makes.
Once specialised, a cell is usually very good at **one job** but cannot do the jobs of other cells.
In animals, differentiation mainly happens in the **embryo**; in plants it continues in cells made by the meristems.
Differentiated cells usually **cannot divide** as fast (or at all, e.g. red blood cells and most nerve cells).

callouts.p: The process by which cells become specialised to carry out a particular function.

callouts.t: Why genes, not loss of DNA
callouts.p: A specialised cell still contains all the DNA. Differentiation is about which genes are expressed, not about losing genes.

core.p: Differentiation is important because a multicellular organism needs **many different jobs** done at the same time: carrying oxygen, sending impulses, contracting, absorbing water, photosynthesising. A single cell type cannot be good at all of these. By making **specialised cells**, the organism gets cells that do each job **efficiently**, and those cells can work together.
bullets: **Division of labour**: different cells share the work of the organism.
Specialised cells with the same function are grouped into **tissues** (e.g. muscle tissue, xylem).
Several tissues working together form an **organ** (e.g. heart, leaf).
Organs working together form an **organ system** (e.g. circulatory system), and organ systems make up the **organism**.
Without differentiation, a large organism would just be a ball of identical cells and could not survive.

callouts.p: Specialised cells, then tissues, then organs, then organ systems, then the whole organism.

core.h: Specialised animal cells: sperm and egg
core.p: Gametes are classic examples of specialised cells. Both have a **haploid nucleus** (one set of chromosomes, 23 in humans) so that when they fuse at fertilisation the zygote is **diploid**. Their other features are adaptations to getting the two nuclei together and supporting the early embryo.
bullets: **Sperm cell: acrosome** at the tip of the head contains **enzymes** that digest the outer layers (jelly coat) of the egg so the sperm can get in.
**Sperm cell: haploid nucleus** carries the father's genetic information.
**Sperm cell: many mitochondria** in the midpiece release **energy by respiration** for the tail to move.
**Sperm cell: flagellum (tail)** lashes to make the sperm **swim** towards the egg.
**Sperm cell**: streamlined, with very little cytoplasm, so it is small and light.
**Egg cell: cytoplasm full of nutrients** (stored food) to supply energy and materials for the early embryo until the placenta forms.
**Egg cell: haploid nucleus** carries the mother's genetic information.
**Egg cell: the cell membrane changes after fertilisation** so that **no more sperm can enter**, ensuring the zygote has the right number of chromosomes.
**Egg cell** is very large compared with a sperm because of its food store.

callouts.p: Say the acrosome contains enzymes that digest / break down the outer layer of the egg.

core.h: Specialised animal cells: ciliated epithelial cells and others
core.p: **Ciliated epithelial cells** line the **trachea and bronchi** and the **oviducts**. On their surface are many tiny hair-like **cilia** that **beat in a coordinated wave** to **move substances** along the surface. In the airways they sweep **mucus**, which has trapped dust and microorganisms, up to the throat to be swallowed. In the oviduct they move the **egg cell** towards the uterus.
bullets: Cilia need energy to beat, so these cells contain **many mitochondria**.
Nearby **goblet cells** make the mucus that the cilia move.
**Red blood cells**: no nucleus and a biconcave disc shape, giving more room for **haemoglobin** and a large surface area for oxygen to diffuse.
**Nerve cells (neurones)**: long axons to carry impulses over long distances, with branched endings to connect to many cells (2.13).
**Muscle cells**: contain protein fibres that contract, and many mitochondria for energy.

head: Specialised cell
Key feature
How it helps the function
rows: Digests outer layer of egg so sperm can enter
Release energy for the flagellum to swim
Beat to move mucus or the egg cell

core.p: Plant cells made in the meristem also differentiate into many types. Each has a structure that matches its function, which is a common exam theme across topics.
bullets: **Root hair cell**: long hair-like extension gives a **large surface area** to absorb water by osmosis and mineral ions by active transport; many mitochondria for active transport; **no chloroplasts** because it is underground.
**Palisade mesophyll cell**: packed with **chloroplasts**, near the top of the leaf, to absorb light for **photosynthesis**.
**Xylem**: cells die and lose their end walls, forming **hollow tubes** strengthened by **lignin**, to carry water and minerals up from roots.
**Phloem**: sieve tube cells with **sieve plates** and few organelles, supported by **companion cells** with many mitochondria, to transport **sucrose** (translocation).
**Guard cells**: change shape to open and close **stomata**.

callouts.p: Always link a feature to its job using 'so that' or 'which means'. A list of features without functions scores poorly.

core.h: Comparing growth in plants and animals
core.p: Examiners like to ask you to **compare** growth in plants and animals. The key ideas are **where** growth happens, **which processes** are involved, and **how long** cells keep the ability to differentiate.
bullets: Plants grow mainly at **tips** (meristems); animals grow **all over** the body.
Plants use **elongation**; animals do not.
Plant meristem cells can differentiate into **any** plant cell **throughout life**; most animal cells differentiate **early** and lose that ability.
Plants keep growing **all their lives**; animals usually **stop growing** as adults.
Both use **mitosis** to make new cells and **differentiation** to specialise them.

callouts.p: Because meristems stay active, plants can regrow whole organs. Most animals can only repair tissues, not regrow organs.

core.h: Exam skills: measuring and calculating growth
core.p: Questions on growth often give data on **length or mass** of seedlings or animals and ask you to calculate **growth rate** or **percentage change**, or to evaluate the **method**.
bullets: Growth rate = change in length or mass / time, with units such as **mm per day** or **g per week**.
Percentage change = (final - initial) / initial x 100.
Use **percentage change** when organisms start at **different sizes**, so results can be compared fairly.
Use **dry mass** for the most valid measure of growth in plants (dry at about 100 degrees C and reweigh until mass is constant).
Repeat with **many organisms** and calculate a **mean** to reduce the effect of individual variation.

callouts.p: Heat and reweigh until two readings are the same, so you know all the water has gone.

analogy.t: A building company and its workers
analogy.p: Think of a new organism as a construction company. At first everyone is a **general trainee** (unspecialised cells). The company **hires more trainees** (cell division), then sends each one on a **training course** where they read only the chapters of the company manual they need (genes switched on): some become electricians, some plumbers, some bricklayers (differentiation into specialised cells). Workers with the same trade form **teams** (tissues), teams work together on **departments** (organs), and departments make up the company (organism). A plant is like a company that keeps a **trainee school open forever** (meristems) and can also make a room bigger just by **inflating it** (elongation). Where it breaks down: real workers can retrain for a new trade, but most specialised animal cells cannot change type; and every cell carries the whole manual, not just its chapters.

terms.d: A permanent increase in the size or mass of an organism.
Production of new cells by mitosis, increasing the number of cells.
Increase in length of a plant cell as its vacuole takes in water by osmosis.
The process by which a cell becomes specialised to carry out a particular function.
A cell with a structure adapted to carry out a particular function.
Region of unspecialised, dividing cells at the tips of plant roots and shoots.
The region just behind a meristem where new plant cells get longer.
A group of similar specialised cells working together to perform a particular function.
A structure made of several different tissues working together to perform a function.
A group of organs working together to carry out a function for the organism.
A nucleus with one set of chromosomes (23 in humans), found in gametes.
Structure in the head of a sperm containing enzymes that digest the outer layers of the egg.
Long tail of a sperm cell that moves it towards the egg.
Tiny hair-like structures on ciliated epithelial cells that beat to move substances such as mucus.
Mass of an organism after all its water has been removed; the most reliable measure of growth.
(Final value - initial value) / initial value x 100; used to compare growth of organisms of different starting size.

mistakes.w: Animals grow by cell division, elongation and differentiation.
mistakes.r: Animals grow by cell division and differentiation only; elongation is a plant process.

mistakes.w: Specialised cells have different genes from each other.
mistakes.r: All body cells have the same genes; in differentiation different genes are switched on or off.

mistakes.w: Plant cells elongate by dividing many times.
mistakes.r: Elongation is when a cell gets longer by taking in water into its vacuole by osmosis; the cell does not divide.

mistakes.w: Meristems are found all over the plant.
mistakes.r: Meristems are at the tips of roots and shoots (and a ring in the stem).

mistakes.w: The acrosome helps the sperm swim.
mistakes.r: The acrosome contains enzymes to digest the outer layer of the egg; the flagellum (tail) and mitochondria allow swimming.

mistakes.w: The egg cell has nutrients to feed the sperm.
mistakes.r: The egg's cytoplasm contains nutrients for the early embryo after fertilisation.

mistakes.w: Mitochondria in a sperm make energy.
mistakes.r: Mitochondria release energy by respiration (energy cannot be made).

mistakes.w: Wet mass is the best measure of growth.
mistakes.r: Dry mass is the most reliable because water content changes, though it kills the organism.

mistakes.w: Cilia move dust out of the lungs by themselves.
mistakes.r: Mucus traps dust and microorganisms, and the cilia beat to sweep the mucus up to the throat.

exam.q: State what is meant by cell differentiation.
model: The process by which a cell becomes specialised (to carry out a particular function).
exam.tip: 'Specialised' is the key word.

exam.q: Name the region of a plant where cells divide rapidly by mitosis.
model: Meristem (at root or shoot tip).
exam.tip: Do not write 'stem cells' for plants.

exam.q: Give two ways in which growth in plants differs from growth in animals.
model: Plants grow by cell elongation, animals do not.
Plant cells (in meristems) can differentiate throughout life, but most animal cells differentiate early / lose the ability.
Plant growth happens mainly at tips; animal growth occurs all over the body.
Plants grow throughout life; animals stop growing as adults.
exam.tip: Make each point a direct comparison.

exam.q: Explain how cell elongation causes a root to grow longer.
model: Water enters the cell / vacuole by osmosis.
The cell expands / gets longer (without dividing), pushing the root tip forward.
exam.tip: Mention osmosis and vacuole.

exam.q: Explain how a sperm cell is adapted to its function.
model: Acrosome contains enzymes to digest the outer layer of the egg.
Haploid nucleus so the zygote has the correct (diploid) number of chromosomes.
Many mitochondria to release energy (by respiration).
Flagellum / tail to swim to the egg.
exam.tip: Feature plus function for each mark.

exam.q: Explain two ways in which an egg cell is adapted for its function.
model: Cytoplasm contains nutrients.
To supply the growing embryo with energy / materials.
Cell membrane changes after fertilisation.
So that only one sperm can enter / no more sperm enter.
exam.tip: Two features, each explained.

exam.q: Describe the role of ciliated epithelial cells in the trachea.
model: Cilia beat / waft.
Moving mucus (containing trapped dust or microorganisms) up and away from the lungs.
exam.tip: Mucus is trapped by goblet cell secretions; cilia move it.

exam.q: Explain why cell differentiation is important in the development of a multicellular organism.
model: Produces specialised cells with different structures.
Each type of cell carries out a particular function efficiently.
Specialised cells form tissues, organs and organ systems so the organism can carry out all life processes.
exam.tip: Link specialisation to tissues and organs.

exam.q: Suggest why dry mass is a better measure of plant growth than wet mass.
model: Water content of a plant varies (e.g. with how recently it was watered).
Dry mass measures only the permanent increase in material / biomass.
exam.tip: Also be ready to say a disadvantage: the plant is killed.

exam.q: A seedling grew from 24 mm to 54 mm in 6 days. Calculate the percentage increase in length.
exam.tip: Divide by the starting value, not the final one.

exam.q: Describe and explain how a plant grows from a seedling into a mature plant with roots, stems and leaves.
model: Cells in meristems at root and shoot tips divide by mitosis.
Mitosis produces many new genetically identical cells.
Just behind the meristem, cells elongate as water enters their vacuoles by osmosis.
Elongation increases the length of the root / shoot.
Further back, cells differentiate into specialised cells, e.g. root hair, xylem, phloem, palisade cells.
Differentiation happens because different genes are switched on.
Specialised cells form tissues and organs (roots, stems, leaves).
Meristem cells stay unspecialised so growth continues throughout life.
exam.tip: Use the order division, elongation, differentiation and give named examples of specialised cells.

worked.q: A student measured the dry mass of samples of seedlings: 2.5 g on day 0 and 3.4 g on day 6. Calculate (a) the mean growth rate in g per day and (b) the percentage increase in dry mass.
steps: (a) Change in mass = 3.4 - 2.5 = 0.9 g.
Growth rate = 0.9 g / 6 days = 0.15 g per day.
(b) Percentage increase = change / starting mass x 100.
worked.ans: (a) 0.15 g per day. (b) 36% increase.

worked.q: Two plants were grown for 10 days. Plant A grew from 40 mm to 60 mm; plant B grew from 10 mm to 25 mm. Which plant had the greater relative growth? Show your working.
steps: Plant A increase = 60 - 40 = 20 mm; percentage = 20 / 40 x 100 = 50%.
Plant B increase = 25 - 10 = 15 mm; percentage = 15 / 10 x 100 = 150%.
Plant A grew more millimetres, but it started bigger.
Percentage change allows a fair comparison of different starting sizes.
worked.ans: Plant B had the greater relative growth (150% compared with 50%).

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why a cell in a root hair zone and a cell in the meristem look so different, even though they contain the same DNA.
steps: Both cells were produced by mitosis, so they have identical DNA / genes.
The meristem cell is unspecialised: small, thin walled, no large vacuole, dividing rapidly.
As the root grew, the older cell moved into the elongation zone, took in water and lengthened.
It then differentiated: some genes were switched on and others switched off.
This produced a long root hair extension giving a large surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions.
worked.ans: They contain the same genes, but in the root hair cell different genes have been switched on during differentiation, so it has developed a structure (long extension, large surface area, no chloroplasts) suited to absorption, while the meristem cell remains unspecialised.

bio_edx.1.4.summary: Doctors and health visitors use **percentile charts** to check that a baby or child is growing normally. The chart shows curved **percentile lines** made from measurements of thousands of healthy children; the **50th percentile** is the middle (median) value, and a child on the **25th percentile** is heavier (or longer) than 25% of children of the same age and sex. **Mass, length (height) and head circumference** are measured regularly and plotted against age. A child growing steadily along roughly the same line is usually healthy; a child whose measurements **cross two or more percentile lines**, sit **above the top or below the bottom line**, or are very **inconsistent between measurements** may need to be investigated.

core.p: A **percentile chart** (growth chart) is a graph of a body measurement, such as **mass**, against **age**. It has several curved lines called **percentile lines**. Each line shows the value below which a given **percentage** of children of that age fall. The lines were drawn from measurements of a very **large number of healthy children**, so the chart shows the normal **range** of growth in the population.
bullets: The **x-axis** is age (weeks, months or years); the **y-axis** is the measurement (kg, cm).
Common lines in exam charts: **5th, 25th, 50th, 75th, 95th**. UK NHS charts use 0.4th, 2nd, 9th, 25th, 50th, 75th, 91st, 98th and 99.6th.
The **50th percentile** is the **median**: half the children are below it and half above it.
The lines **curve upwards** steeply in the first months, because babies grow fastest early on, then flatten.
The lines **spread apart** with age, because children vary more as they get older.

callouts.p: The value below which a given percentage of a population falls. A baby on the 75th percentile for mass is heavier than 75% of babies of the same age and sex.

core.p: The percentile tells you a child's **position compared with other children** of the **same age and sex**. Think of 100 babies of the same age lined up from lightest to heaviest. A baby on the **25th percentile** is the 25th in the line: **25% are lighter** and **75% are heavier**. A baby on the 95th percentile is heavier than 95% of babies, so only 5% are heavier.
bullets: Percentage of children **above** a line = 100 - percentile. On the 91st percentile, 9% are heavier.
Percentage **between** two lines = difference between them. Between the 25th and 75th lies **50%** of children.
Being on a low or high percentile is **not** a problem by itself: someone has to be on every line, and small parents tend to have small babies.
Percentile is about **rank**, not about health or how much the child weighs in kg.

callouts.p: 'What percentage of babies are heavier?' needs 100 minus the percentile. 'Lighter' is the percentile itself.

core.p: Babies and young children have three main measurements plotted on separate percentile charts. Measuring several things gives a **fuller picture** of growth, because problems may show in one measurement before the others.
bullets: **Mass (weight)** in kg: shows whether the baby is getting enough nutrition; affected quickly by feeding problems or illness.
**Length** (lying down, for babies) or **height** (standing, for older children) in cm: shows long-term growth of the skeleton.
**Head circumference** in cm: measured around the widest part of the head; it reflects **brain growth**, so it is checked carefully in the first year.
Measurements are taken at **regular intervals** (birth, then at checks in the first weeks and months) and recorded in the child's health record (the 'red book' in the UK).
Each measurement is plotted against age as a **point**; joining the points shows the child's own **growth curve**.

head: Measurement
Unit
Mainly shows
rows: Growth of the brain and skull

callouts.p: There are separate charts for boys and girls, because boys are on average slightly heavier and longer at the same age.

core.h: Normal growth on a percentile chart
core.p: What matters most is the **pattern** of growth over time, not a single point. A healthy child usually grows along a path **roughly parallel to the percentile lines**, staying on or near the **same percentile** as they get older. Small ups and downs are normal (for example after a cold or a growth spurt).
bullets: A baby born on the 25th percentile who stays near the 25th is growing **normally** for that baby.
Babies often lose a little mass in the **first few days** after birth and regain it by about 2 weeks.
Children tend to stay on similar percentiles for **mass, length and head circumference**.
**Genes** affect percentile: tall parents tend to have children on higher height percentiles.

callouts.p: Staying close to one percentile line, even a low one, usually shows healthy growth.

core.p: Percentile charts are a **screening tool**: they help doctors spot children who **may** have a problem so they can be checked more closely. Doctors are most concerned when the **pattern** changes or the measurement is extreme.
bullets: **Crossing two or more percentile lines** (moving up or down a lot) over a short time, for example dropping from the 75th to the 9th for mass.
Measurements **below the lowest line or above the highest line**, which affects very few healthy children.
**Inconsistency** between measurements, for example mass on the 9th percentile but head circumference on the 98th.
**Growth stopping** (a flat line) while the percentile lines keep rising.
A sudden increase in **head circumference** can suggest fluid building up on the brain (hydrocephalus).

head: Pattern seen
Possible cause to investigate
rows: Poor feeding, malnutrition, infection, digestive problem
Hormone (e.g. growth hormone) problem, long-term illness
Possible illness or genetic condition, or simply small parents

callouts.p: A percentile chart cannot say what is wrong. It only shows that growth is unusual, so further tests are needed.

core.h: How to read a percentile chart
core.p: Exam questions often give a chart and ask you to read off a value or a percentile. Use a ruler and work step by step.
bullets: Find the child's **age** on the x-axis and draw a line straight **up**.
Find the **measurement** on the y-axis and draw a line straight **across**.
Where the lines meet, see which **percentile line** the point is on or between.
If it is between two lines, say 'between the 25th and 50th percentile'.
To find the expected value for a percentile, go up from the age to the percentile line, then across to the y-axis.
Always give **units** for values read from the axis (kg or cm).

callouts.p: Count how many units each small square represents before reading a value. Many errors come from misreading the scale.

core.p: Regular measurement allows **early detection** of problems. Many conditions that affect growth can be treated more successfully if they are found early, and parents can be **reassured** when growth is normal.
bullets: Detects **malnutrition** or feeding problems early, so feeding can be changed.
Can reveal illnesses such as infections, coeliac disease or heart problems that slow growth.
Spots unusually **rapid weight gain**, which could lead to childhood **obesity**.
Detects possible **hormone** or **genetic** conditions affecting height.
Head circumference checks can detect brain development problems early.
Allows comparison with a **large reference population**, rather than just with siblings or friends.

core.p: Charts are very useful, but a grade 9 answer should also say what they **cannot** do. The chart only compares a child with a reference population.
bullets: They show **unusual growth**, not the **cause**; further tests are needed.
A child can be healthy and still be on a very low or very high percentile because of **genetics** (small or tall parents).
Single measurements can be **inaccurate** (baby wriggling, clothes or nappy on, different scales), so trends over several measurements are more reliable.
The reference data may come from a population with different **ethnic background, diet or era**, so it may not match every child.
**Premature babies** must be plotted using **corrected age** (age from due date), or they look too small.
Breast-fed and formula-fed babies grow slightly differently; UK charts are based on WHO data from healthy **breast-fed** babies.

callouts.p: One reading tells you little. A series of readings showing the child's path across the chart is what matters.

core.h: Putting it into practice: health checks
core.p: In the UK, a baby is weighed and measured at birth and then at regular health checks. A **health visitor** plots the values on the charts in the child's record. If something unusual shows up, the baby is weighed more often, and may be **referred to a doctor** (GP or paediatrician).
bullets: Measurements are **plotted, not just recorded**, so trends can be seen at a glance.
More frequent checks are done if the baby was **premature**, ill, or had feeding problems.
Older children may have height and weight checked at school, and their **BMI** compared with BMI percentile charts.
The same chart idea is used for **BMI-for-age** in children because adult BMI categories do not suit growing bodies.
