core.p: Several types of calculation come up. They usually use values read from the chart, so be careful reading the graph first.
bullets: **Change in mass** = later mass - earlier mass (in kg).
**Rate of growth** = change in mass / time, e.g. kg per month.
**Percentage increase** = (final - initial) / initial x 100, e.g. from birth mass.
**Percentage of babies above** a value = 100 - percentile.
**Number of babies** in a group on or below a percentile = percentile / 100 x group size.

callouts.p: Calculation questions usually give a mark for working even if the final answer is wrong.

core.h: Links to other parts of Topic 2
core.p: Growth on a percentile chart is the result of the cell processes covered in the rest of the topic.
bullets: Increase in mass and length comes from **cell division by mitosis** and **cell differentiation** (2.1-2.6).
Growth is fastest in the **first year**, when cells divide rapidly.
Abnormal growth patterns can be linked to problems with cell division, hormones or nutrition.
Percentile charts monitor **whole-body growth**, while the cell cycle explains growth at the **cell level**.

analogy.t: Your place in a running race
analogy.p: Think of all the babies born on the same day as runners in a long race, with mass as distance covered. The percentile is your **position in the pack**: on the 25th percentile, a quarter of runners are behind you. Running steadily in the same position is fine, even near the back. What worries the race officials is a runner who suddenly **drops back through lots of other runners** (crossing percentile lines) or one who is **far off the back or front of the pack**. Where it breaks down: in a race being ahead is better, but on a growth chart a higher percentile is not 'better'; and children are not competing, because genes set where each child naturally sits.

terms.d: A graph showing the distribution of a body measurement (e.g. mass) against age for a large population, used to monitor growth.
The value below which a given percentage of the population falls.
A curve on a growth chart joining the values for one percentile at each age.
The middle value: half the children of that age are below it and half are above it.
A permanent increase in size or mass of an organism.
Distance around the widest part of the head; an indicator of brain growth.
Body measurement of a baby taken lying down, from head to heel.
Measure of how heavy the baby is, in kg; shows nutrition and general health.
A child's measurements moving up or down across two or more percentile lines; a warning sign.
The large group of healthy children whose measurements were used to draw the percentile lines.
Age of a premature baby counted from the due date, used when plotting on growth charts.
Nurse who checks young children's growth and development and plots measurements on percentile charts.
Not getting the right amount of nutrients; may show as mass falling across percentile lines.
Build up of fluid on the brain; may show as head circumference rising across percentile lines.

mistakes.w: A baby on the 25th percentile is 25% underweight.
mistakes.r: A baby on the 25th percentile is heavier than 25% of babies of the same age and sex (and lighter than 75%).

mistakes.w: A baby on the 5th percentile must be unhealthy.
mistakes.r: Low percentile alone is not a problem; concern arises if the baby crosses lines, is below the lowest line, or measurements are inconsistent.

mistakes.w: The 50th percentile is the mean.
mistakes.r: The 50th percentile is the median: half of children are below and half above it.

mistakes.w: A higher percentile means a healthier baby.
mistakes.r: Percentile shows position in the population, not health. Rapid rise across lines can be a problem too.

mistakes.w: Doctors look at one measurement to decide if a baby is growing well.
mistakes.r: Doctors look at the trend over several measurements and compare mass, length and head circumference.

mistakes.w: The same chart is used for boys and girls.
mistakes.r: Separate charts are used because boys and girls grow differently on average.

mistakes.w: On the 91st percentile, 91% of babies are heavier.
mistakes.r: 91% are lighter; 100 - 91 = 9% are heavier.

mistakes.w: Percentile charts tell you what is wrong with the baby.
mistakes.r: They only show unusual growth so that the cause can be investigated with further tests.

exam.q: State what is meant by the 50th percentile on a growth chart.
model: The median / middle value: 50% of babies (of that age) have a lower measurement and 50% higher.
exam.tip: Use 'median', not 'mean' or 'average' alone.

exam.q: Give two measurements of a baby that are plotted on percentile charts.
model: Mass / weight.
Length / height.
Head circumference.
exam.tip: Any two.

exam.q: A baby is on the 75th percentile for mass. State what percentage of babies of the same age are heavier than this baby.
Explain why boys and girls have separate percentile charts.
model: Boys and girls grow at different rates / boys are on average heavier and longer.
So comparing a child with the correct sex gives a valid comparison.
exam.tip: Talk about fair comparison.

exam.q: Explain why head circumference is measured in young babies.
model: It shows growth of the brain (and skull).
Abnormal increase or decrease can indicate a problem (e.g. hydrocephalus) that needs early treatment.
exam.tip: Link to the brain.

exam.q: A baby's mass was on the 50th percentile at birth, the 25th at 3 months and below the 5th at 6 months. Explain why the doctor is concerned.
model: The baby has crossed two or more percentile lines / has dropped from the 50th to below the 5th.
Shows the baby is not gaining mass as expected, suggesting a problem such as poor feeding / malnutrition / illness.
exam.tip: Describe the pattern, then suggest a cause.

exam.q: Suggest why a baby that stays on the 9th percentile for mass, length and head circumference may still be healthy.
model: The baby is growing steadily along one percentile line / following the curve.
Measurements are consistent with each other; the baby may have small parents (genetic).
exam.tip: Consistency plus genetics.

exam.q: Give two reasons why doctors monitor the growth of babies using percentile charts.
model: To detect problems with growth / development early.
So treatment can be given early (e.g. for malnutrition or illness).
To reassure parents that growth is normal.
exam.tip: Early detection is the key idea.

exam.q: A baby's mass increased from 3.5 kg at birth to 7.7 kg at 6 months. Calculate the percentage increase in mass.
exam.tip: Divide by the birth mass.

exam.q: Evaluate the use of percentile charts to monitor the growth of children.
model: Charts compare a child with a large reference population of healthy children of the same age and sex.
Regular plotting shows the child's trend over time, not just one value.
Crossing two or more lines, or being outside the range, flags a possible problem.
Allows early detection and treatment of malnutrition, illness or hormone problems; reassures parents.
But a chart cannot identify the cause; further tests are needed.
A child may be healthy on a low or high percentile due to genetics.
Measurement errors (wriggling baby, clothes) can give misleading points.
Reference population may not match every child (ethnicity, premature, feeding type), so corrected age or other charts may be needed.
Conclusion: a useful screening tool when used with several measurements over time.
exam.tip: For 'evaluate', give advantages AND limitations and finish with a judgement.

worked.q: In a clinic, 240 baby girls of the same age were measured. How many would you expect to have a mass below the 25th percentile, and how many above the 91st percentile?
steps: Below the 25th percentile means the lightest 25% of babies.
Above the 91st percentile means the heaviest 100 - 91 = 9%.
9 / 100 x 240 = 21.6, so about 22 babies.
worked.ans: About 60 babies below the 25th percentile and about 22 babies above the 91st percentile.

worked.q: A baby boy had a mass of 3.4 kg at birth (50th percentile). At 4 months his mass was 5.4 kg; the 50th percentile at 4 months is 7.0 kg and the 5th percentile is 5.6 kg. Calculate his mean growth rate and comment on his growth.
steps: Change in mass = 5.4 - 3.4 = 2.0 kg.
Growth rate = 2.0 kg / 4 months = 0.5 kg per month.
At 4 months he is 5.4 kg, which is below the 5th percentile (5.6 kg).
He has dropped from the 50th percentile to below the 5th, crossing several percentile lines.
worked.ans: Mean growth rate = 0.5 kg per month. He has crossed several percentile lines and is now below the 5th percentile, so his growth is a concern and a doctor should investigate (e.g. feeding problems or illness).

worked.q: Model answer: A baby's mass is on the 25th percentile and length is on the 25th percentile, but head circumference has risen from the 50th to above the 98th percentile in 2 months. Explain what the health visitor should conclude.
steps: Mass and length are consistent and on the same line, so general growth looks normal.
Head circumference has crossed several percentile lines in a short time.
Head circumference is now inconsistent with mass and length.
A rapid rise in head size could indicate fluid building up around the brain (hydrocephalus) or another problem.
The chart cannot diagnose the cause, so the baby should be referred for tests.
worked.ans: Growth in mass and length is normal, but the rapid rise in head circumference across lines and its inconsistency with the other measurements is a warning sign, so the baby should be referred to a doctor for investigation.

bio_edx.1.7.summary: Doctors and scientists cannot simply open the skull to see what is going on inside a living brain, so they use **scans**. A **CT scan** uses many X-ray images taken from different angles to build up detailed **cross-sections showing the structure** of the brain, such as tumours, bleeding or damaged areas. A **PET scan** uses a **radioactive tracer** (usually radioactive glucose) to show **which parts of the brain are active**, so it reveals **function** as well as structure. Comparing scans with a person's symptoms, or watching which areas light up during a task, lets us link brain regions to what they do, but both scans use ionising radiation and have limitations.

core.h: Why we need scans to study the brain
core.p: The brain is protected by the **skull** and is extremely delicate, so cutting into it to investigate is dangerous and can cause permanent damage. Scans are **non-invasive** (or only minimally invasive) ways of looking inside the living brain. Historically, scientists learned what brain areas did by studying people with **brain damage** (from injuries, strokes or tumours) and linking the damaged area, found after death, to the symptoms the person had while alive. Modern scans let us do this while the person is still alive.
bullets: The brain cannot easily be repaired, so investigation must avoid causing new damage.
Scans let doctors **diagnose** problems such as tumours, bleeding and diseases like Alzheimer's.
Scans let scientists **investigate brain function**: which region is linked to which job (memory, language, movement, vision).
The two scans on the Edexcel specification are **CT (computerised tomography)** and **PET (positron emission tomography)**.
Key difference: **CT shows structure**, **PET shows activity (function)**.

callouts.p: CT scan = X-rays = detailed picture of **structure**. PET scan = radioactive tracer = picture of **activity / function**.

core.h: What a CT scan is and how it works
core.p: CT stands for **computerised tomography** (tomography means imaging in slices). The patient lies on a bed that moves through a ring-shaped scanner. An **X-ray source rotates around the head** and fires thin beams of X-rays through it from **many different angles**. **Detectors** on the opposite side measure how much X-ray gets through. A **computer** combines all these measurements to produce detailed **cross-sectional images (slices)** of the brain, which can be stacked to give a 3D picture.
bullets: X-rays are **absorbed by different tissues by different amounts**: dense tissue like **bone** absorbs a lot and looks **white**; soft tissue looks grey; fluid and air look darker.
Because many images are taken from many angles, the computer can work out the position of each structure, giving far more detail than a single ordinary X-ray.
The result is a series of slices, so doctors can see exactly **where** in the brain a problem is.
A CT scan is quick (minutes), widely available and relatively cheap compared with PET.

callouts.p: A scan that uses **X-rays** taken from many angles, combined by a **computer**, to produce detailed **cross-sectional images** of the **structure** of the brain.

fig.cap: Figure 1: A CT scanner. The X-ray tube rotates around the patient's head, detectors on the opposite side measure the X-rays that pass through, and a computer combines the readings into a cross-sectional image (slice) of the brain.

core.h: What a CT scan shows about the brain
core.p: A CT scan gives a picture of the brain's **structure**, not what it is doing. This makes it excellent for spotting **physical damage or abnormal structures**. Doctors look for areas that look different from a normal brain.
bullets: **Tumours**: an abnormal mass of tissue that shows up as a different shade.
**Bleeding (haemorrhage)**, for example after a head injury or a stroke caused by a burst blood vessel; fresh blood shows up brighter than brain tissue.
**Damaged or dead tissue**, for example after a stroke caused by a blocked blood vessel.
**Skull fractures**, because bone shows up clearly.
Changes in the size of fluid-filled spaces, or **shrinkage of brain tissue**.

callouts.p: A CT scan does **not** show which parts of the brain are active. If the question asks about activity or function during a task, the answer is **PET**, not CT.

fig.cap: Figure 2: What a doctor might see on a CT slice of the brain. Bone of the skull shows up white, fresh blood from a bleed is bright, a tumour shows as an abnormal mass and the fluid-filled spaces are dark. The scan shows where structures are, not how active they are.

core.h: Advantages and disadvantages of CT scans
core.p: Like any medical test, CT scans have benefits and risks, and exam questions often ask you to evaluate them.
bullets: **Advantage**: gives very detailed images of structure, so tumours, bleeds and damaged areas can be located precisely before surgery or treatment.
**Advantage**: fast, so it is used in emergencies such as head injuries and suspected strokes.
**Advantage**: cheaper and more widely available than PET.
**Disadvantage**: uses **X-rays, which are ionising radiation**. Ionising radiation can damage DNA and slightly **increase the risk of cancer**, so the number of scans is kept as low as possible.
**Disadvantage**: shows **structure only**, not activity, so a brain that looks normal on CT may still be working abnormally (for example early Alzheimer's).
**Disadvantage**: the patient must keep very still; images are less detailed for some soft tissues than other methods.

callouts.p: For a balanced answer give at least one advantage and one disadvantage of each scan and finish with a judgement, for example that the benefit of diagnosis usually outweighs the small radiation risk.

core.h: What a PET scan is and how it works
core.p: PET stands for **positron emission tomography**. Before the scan the patient is **injected with a radioactive tracer**, usually a form of **glucose** that has been made radioactive (labelled with a radioactive atom). The tracer travels in the **blood** to the brain. **Active brain cells respire more**, so they **take up more glucose** and therefore **more tracer**. The tracer emits radiation, which is detected by the scanner, and a **computer** turns this into a **colour-coded image** in which the most active areas show up brightest.
bullets: Step 1: radioactive tracer (radioactive glucose) is injected into the blood.
Step 2: blood carries the tracer around the body and to the brain.
Step 3: **more active cells use more glucose for respiration**, so tracer builds up in those areas.
Step 4: the tracer gives off radiation, which is picked up by detectors around the head.
Step 5: a computer produces a colour image; **red and yellow usually show high activity**, blue and purple show low activity.
Because it shows where glucose is being used, PET shows the brain's **function (activity)**, not just its shape.

callouts.p: A scan in which a **radioactive tracer** (radioactive glucose) is injected; **active** areas of the brain absorb more tracer, so the scan shows **which parts of the brain are active**.
Neurones need lots of energy from **respiration**, which uses **glucose**. The harder a brain area is working, the more glucose it takes up, so glucose is the perfect marker of activity.

fig.cap: Figure 3: The stages of a PET scan. A radioactive glucose tracer is injected, carried in the blood to the brain and taken up most by the most active cells, which respire fastest. The radiation it gives off is detected and a computer builds a colour map where bright colours mean high activity.

core.h: What PET scans show: function and disease
core.p: Because PET shows activity, it can reveal problems that do not change the brain's shape, and it can show which areas are used for different tasks.
bullets: **Alzheimer's disease and dementia**: areas involved in memory show **reduced activity** (less glucose used) because neurones are damaged or dying. PET can detect this **earlier** than CT, before much tissue has been lost.
**Tumours**: many tumour cells divide rapidly and respire a lot, so they take up more tracer and show as **unusually active** areas.
**Research**: a volunteer does a task (reading, listening to music, moving a hand, remembering a list) during the scan; the areas that **light up** are the ones used for that task.
**Comparing** scans of healthy people with those of patients shows which areas are not working normally.
Repeated PET scans can show whether a treatment is working, for example whether a tumour becomes less active.

callouts.p: If an area of the brain is consistently more active whenever a person performs a particular task, that area is likely to be **involved in that function**.

fig.cap: Figure 4: Simplified PET images of the brain viewed from above. In the healthy brain many areas are bright (high glucose use). In Alzheimer's disease large areas, especially those used for memory, are blue and purple, showing reduced activity because neurones are damaged.

core.h: Advantages and disadvantages of PET scans
core.p: PET gives information that CT cannot, but it is more limited in other ways.
bullets: **Advantage**: shows **activity / function**, so it can detect diseases such as Alzheimer's that change how the brain works before its structure changes much.
**Advantage**: can be used in research to **map functions** to brain regions in living, healthy people.

**Disadvantage**: the tracer is **radioactive**, so the patient is exposed to **ionising radiation**, which can damage cells and slightly increases cancer risk. This limits how often one person can be scanned.
**Disadvantage**: the tracer must be **injected**, so it is slightly invasive.
**Disadvantage**: the tracers are short-lived and must be made shortly before use, so PET is **very expensive** and only available in some hospitals.
**Disadvantage**: images are **less detailed** for structure than CT, so the two scans are often combined (a PET-CT scan).

callouts.p: PET shows that an area is **active during** a task; it does not by itself prove that the area **causes** the behaviour. Areas can be active for other reasons.

core.p: The most common exam question asks you to compare the two scans. Learn this table.
bullets: Use CT when you need to know **where** something physical is (tumour, bleed, fracture).
Use PET when you need to know **how well** parts of the brain are **working**.
Both use **ionising radiation**, so both carry a small risk; doctors weigh the benefit of the information against the risk.

callouts.p: In a compare question each mark point needs **both scans** in the same sentence, for example: CT shows structure **whereas** PET shows activity.

core.h: Linking scans to brain regions (cerebrum, cerebellum, medulla)
core.p: Scans are how we know which part of the brain does which job. When a scan shows damage or reduced activity in one region, doctors can predict symptoms, and when a person has symptoms, the scan shows where to look.
bullets: Damage in the **cerebrum** (for example after a stroke) can affect movement on one side of the body, speech, memory, vision or personality, depending on exactly where.
Damage to the **cerebellum** may cause poor balance and clumsy, uncoordinated movement.
Damage to the **medulla oblongata** can affect unconscious activities such as breathing and heart rate and is often life-threatening.
PET research shows, for example, that areas at the **back of the cerebrum are active when we look at things**, and areas involved in speech and language become active when we talk.
Combining a CT scan (where the damage is) with the person's symptoms (what they can no longer do) links structure to function.

callouts.p: If you are shown a scan and told the symptoms, say which region is affected and explain using the function of that region.

core.h: Scans in diagnosis and planning treatment
core.p: Scans do not treat anything themselves, but they make treatment safer and more accurate.
bullets: A CT scan shows the **exact position and size of a tumour**, helping surgeons plan how to remove it while damaging as little healthy tissue as possible.
After a stroke, CT quickly shows whether it was caused by **bleeding** or a **blockage**; this matters because the treatments are different.
PET can show whether a tumour is still active after treatment.
PET can support a diagnosis of Alzheimer's or other dementias, helping patients and families plan care.
Scans can be **repeated over time** to monitor how a disease progresses, but each scan adds to the radiation dose.

core.p: Using scans raises questions you may be asked to discuss in longer answers.
bullets: **Risk versus benefit**: radiation exposure is justified for diagnosis but harder to justify for research on healthy volunteers, who gain no medical benefit.
**Consent**: volunteers and patients must give informed consent; this can be difficult for people with severe dementia.
**Cost**: PET is expensive, so health services must decide who should get scans.
**Incidental findings**: a research scan may reveal an unexpected problem, raising the question of whether and how to tell the volunteer.
**Limited conclusions**: a scan shows a snapshot; it cannot always predict how a person's condition will develop.

callouts.p: CT uses X-rays and PET uses a radioactive tracer, so **both expose the patient to ionising radiation**. Pregnant women and children are scanned only when really needed.

core.p: Questions on CT and PET are usually 2 to 6 marks and test whether you can explain how each scan works, what it shows and when you would use it.
bullets: Always state the **source of the image**: X-rays for CT; radioactive tracer for PET.
For PET explain the **chain**: active cells **respire more**, so use **more glucose**, so take up **more tracer**, so appear **brighter**.
For a choice of scan, justify it: CT for structure / location of damage; PET for activity / function.
Mention **ionising radiation** as the main risk of both.
In 6-mark questions on investigating brain function, describe the method (task during scan, compare with control), what the scan shows, and a limitation.

callouts.p: Write **radioactive tracer** or **radioactive glucose**, not just dye or chemical. Write **X-rays**, not radio waves or ultrasound.

analogy.p: A CT scan is like an **aerial map of a city in daylight**: it shows every road and building in detail, including a collapsed bridge (a tumour or bleed), but tells you nothing about what people are doing. A PET scan is like a **satellite photo at night**: you cannot see the buildings clearly, but the bright lights show which areas are busy right now. A district that has gone dark (low activity, as in Alzheimer's) stands out even if its buildings still look normal. Where it breaks down: city lights are switched on deliberately, whereas a PET scan shows brightness only because busy brain cells absorb more radioactive glucose; and making these brain pictures exposes the person to ionising radiation, which a photo of a city does not.

terms.d: Computerised tomography: X-rays passed through the head from many angles and combined by a computer to give cross-sectional images of brain structure.
Positron emission tomography: a scan using an injected radioactive tracer to show which areas of the brain are most active.
High-energy, ionising electromagnetic waves that pass through soft tissue but are absorbed more by dense tissue such as bone.
A substance containing a radioactive atom that is injected into the body so that where it goes can be detected; in PET it is usually radioactive glucose.
The sugar used by cells in respiration; more active brain cells take up more glucose.
The chemical process in cells that releases energy from glucose; very active neurones respire at a high rate.
Radiation (such as X-rays and radiation from radioactive tracers) that can damage DNA in cells and increase the risk of cancer.
An image of a thin slice through the brain, as produced by CT scanning.
The physical make-up and shape of the brain: its regions, tissues and any abnormal masses or damage.
What a part of the brain does, shown by its activity, for example controlling movement or memory.
An abnormal mass of cells formed by uncontrolled cell division.
Bleeding, for example from a burst blood vessel in the brain.
Damage to part of the brain caused when its blood supply is interrupted by a blockage or a burst blood vessel.
A disease in which brain neurones are damaged and die, causing memory loss; PET scans show reduced activity in affected areas.
A procedure that does not involve cutting into the body; CT is non-invasive, PET is only minimally invasive because of the injection.
Part of the scanner that measures the X-rays (CT) or radiation from the tracer (PET) leaving the head.

mistakes.w: A CT scan shows which parts of the brain are active.
mistakes.r: A CT scan shows the structure of the brain; a PET scan shows which areas are active.

mistakes.w: PET scans use X-rays.
mistakes.r: PET scans use an injected radioactive tracer (radioactive glucose); CT scans use X-rays.

mistakes.w: The tracer is a dye that makes the brain glow.
mistakes.r: The tracer is radioactive glucose; active cells absorb more of it and the radiation it emits is detected.

mistakes.w: Active areas light up because they have more blood or more neurones.
mistakes.r: Active areas respire more, so they take up more glucose and therefore more tracer.

mistakes.w: CT and PET scans are completely safe.
mistakes.r: Both expose the patient to ionising radiation, which can damage DNA and slightly increase the risk of cancer.

mistakes.w: A PET scan proves a brain area causes a behaviour.
mistakes.r: PET shows the area is active during the task (a correlation); other evidence is needed to show it is responsible.

mistakes.w: Alzheimer's shows as bright areas on PET.
mistakes.r: Alzheimer's shows as areas of reduced activity (less glucose used) because neurones are damaged.

mistakes.w: CT scans can be used to treat tumours.
mistakes.r: Scans are for diagnosis and planning; they show where a tumour is but do not treat it.

exam.q: State what type of radiation is used to produce a CT scan.
model: X-rays
exam.tip: One word answers are fine for 1-mark state questions.

exam.q: What is injected into a patient before a PET scan?
model: A radioactive tracer / radioactive glucose
exam.tip: Must include the idea of radioactive.

exam.q: Give one disadvantage that CT and PET scans have in common.
model: Both expose the patient to ionising radiation which can increase the risk of cancer / damage cells (accept: expensive)
exam.tip: Radiation is the safest answer.

exam.q: Describe how a CT scan produces an image of the brain.
model: X-rays are passed through the head
from many different angles / source rotates around the head
detectors measure the X-rays passing through
a computer combines the information to give cross-sectional images (slices)
exam.tip: Any three of the four points; mention the computer.

exam.q: Explain why areas of the brain that are more active show up brighter on a PET scan.
model: more active neurones respire more
so they take up / use more glucose
so more radioactive tracer (glucose) builds up there
more radiation is detected from these areas
exam.tip: Build a cause-and-effect chain: activity, respiration, glucose, tracer.

exam.q: A patient has had a fall and banged their head. Explain why a doctor would choose a CT scan rather than a PET scan.
model: CT shows the structure of the brain in detail
so can show bleeding / skull fracture / damage
it is quicker / cheaper / more available in an emergency (any one)
exam.tip: Link the choice to the type of problem: physical damage means structure means CT.

exam.q: Compare CT and PET scans as methods of investigating the brain.
model: CT uses X-rays whereas PET uses an injected radioactive tracer
CT shows structure whereas PET shows activity / function
CT gives more detailed images of structure
PET is more expensive / less available
both expose the patient to ionising radiation
exam.tip: Every point should mention both scans, using whereas or but.

exam.q: A PET scan of a patient with memory loss shows less activity in some areas of the cerebrum than the scan of a healthy person. Suggest an explanation.
model: neurones in these areas are damaged / have died (e.g. Alzheimer's disease)
so they respire less / take up less glucose / tracer
these areas are involved in memory
exam.tip: Use the data: less activity means fewer working neurones there.

exam.q: Scientists want to find out which part of the brain is used when people listen to music. Describe how they could use PET scans to do this.
model: inject volunteers with radioactive tracer / glucose
scan the brain while the volunteer listens to music
scan the same person at rest / in silence as a control and compare
the area(s) that are more active / brighter during music are involved
use a large number of volunteers to see if the pattern is repeatable
exam.tip: Treat it like a mini experiment: method, control, comparison, repeats.

exam.q: Evaluate the use of CT and PET scans to investigate brain damage and disease.
model: CT uses X-rays from many angles to produce detailed images of structure
CT can locate tumours / bleeds / stroke damage so surgery can be planned
CT is quick, cheap and widely available
but CT does not show activity / function
PET uses radioactive glucose; active areas take up more tracer
PET shows function so can detect Alzheimer's / early disease before structure changes
but PET is expensive / less detailed / tracer must be injected
both expose patients to ionising radiation so number of scans must be limited
conclusion: the scans are complementary; benefit of diagnosis usually outweighs small risk
exam.tip: Top band answers cover both scans, give pros and cons, and end with a justified conclusion.

exam.q: Suggest why a doctor would want to limit the number of PET scans a patient has.
model: the tracer is radioactive / emits ionising radiation
which can damage DNA / cells and increase the risk of cancer
(accept: expensive)
exam.tip: Explain the harm, not just say radiation.

worked.q: A patient suddenly cannot move the right side of their body. A CT scan shows a dark area in the left side of the cerebrum. Explain what the doctor can conclude and why a CT scan was useful.
steps: Identify what CT shows: the structure of the brain, so the dark area is tissue that looks different from normal.
Link to cause: this suggests an area of damaged or dead tissue, for example from a stroke caused by a blocked blood vessel.
Link to function: the cerebrum controls voluntary movement, and the left side of the cerebrum controls the right side of the body.
Explain usefulness: CT is fast, so the doctor quickly knows the location of the damage and whether it is a bleed or a blockage, which affects treatment.
worked.ans: The scan shows damage to the part of the left cerebrum that controls movement of the right side of the body, probably from a stroke. CT was useful because it quickly shows the structure and exact location of the damage so the right treatment can be chosen.

worked.q: Two volunteers have PET scans. Volunteer A is reading aloud and shows bright areas in two regions of the cerebrum. Volunteer B is resting with eyes closed and those regions are mainly blue. What can the scientists conclude, and what are the limitations?
steps: Explain the colours: bright areas have taken up more radioactive glucose because their cells are respiring more, so they are more active.
Conclusion: these two regions are more active during reading aloud, so they are likely to be involved in vision, language or speech.
Limitation 1: only two people, and different people; scientists should scan the same people in both conditions and use many volunteers.
Limitation 2: activity shows a link (correlation) but does not prove the region causes reading.
Limitation 3: volunteers receive ionising radiation, so the number of scans must be limited.
worked.ans: The regions are probably involved in reading or speaking because they are more active (use more glucose) during the task. The conclusion is weak because the sample is tiny, different people were compared, and PET shows correlation, not proof of cause.

bio_edx.1.8.summary: Damage and disease in the **brain** and **spinal cord** (the central nervous system) are among the hardest medical problems to treat. **Neurones in the central nervous system do not usually repair or replace themselves**, the brain is **delicate, complex and enclosed by the skull**, and the **blood-brain barrier** stops many drugs from reaching brain tissue. This is why **spinal injuries** often cause permanent paralysis and why **brain tumours** can be difficult to remove without damaging healthy tissue. Scientists are researching new treatments such as stem cells, but these are not yet reliable.

core.h: The nervous system and why damage matters
core.p: The **central nervous system (CNS)** is the **brain and spinal cord**. The **peripheral nervous system** is the network of nerves that connects the CNS to the rest of the body. The CNS coordinates everything we do, so damage to even a small area can affect movement, sensation, memory, speech or vital functions like breathing.
bullets: The **cerebrum** controls conscious thought, memory, language and voluntary movement; the **cerebellum** coordinates balance and muscle activity; the **medulla oblongata** controls unconscious activities such as heart rate and breathing.
The **spinal cord** carries impulses between the brain and the body.
Causes of damage include **injuries** (accidents, falls, sports), **strokes**, **tumours** and **diseases** such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and multiple sclerosis.
The effects depend on **where** the damage is, which is why scans are used first to locate it.

callouts.t: The core message of this spec point
callouts.p: Treating the brain and nervous system is **limited** because neurones do not easily regrow, the brain is hard to reach and easily damaged, it is complex and not fully understood, and many drugs cannot get into it.

core.h: Limitation 1: neurones do not easily repair or replace themselves
core.p: Most body tissues repair damage by **mitosis**: cells divide to replace the ones that were lost. Mature **neurones do not divide**, and neurones in the **CNS usually cannot regrow** their long axons once they are cut or crushed. So damage to the brain and spinal cord is often **permanent**.
bullets: Skin, bone and liver can heal because their cells can divide; brain and spinal cord tissue largely cannot.
When neurones die, they are not replaced by new neurones, so lost function is usually not fully restored.
Some nerves in the **peripheral nervous system** can regrow slowly if the cell body is not damaged, but in the **CNS** regrowth is very limited.
Some recovery after a stroke or injury can happen because **other areas of the brain take over** some functions, but this is slow and usually incomplete.

callouts.p: Neurones in the brain and spinal cord **cannot divide by mitosis** and **rarely regrow**, so damaged tissue is not replaced.

core.p: The **spinal cord** is a bundle of neurones running down inside the protective **vertebral column** (backbone). It carries **sensory impulses up** to the brain and **motor impulses down** to muscles. If it is cut or crushed, impulses can no longer pass the damaged point.
bullets: Below the injury the person may have **paralysis** (cannot move muscles) and **loss of sensation** (cannot feel), because messages cannot travel between the brain and that part of the body.
The **higher up** the spinal cord the injury, the **more of the body** is affected; an injury in the neck can affect arms, legs and even breathing.
Because CNS neurones do not regrow, a severed spinal cord **cannot currently be repaired**; treatment focuses on preventing further damage and rehabilitation.
Surgery can stabilise broken vertebrae, but it cannot reconnect the cut neurones.
Reflexes below the injury may still work, because some reflex arcs pass through the spinal cord without needing the brain.

callouts.p: Paralysis after a spinal injury is not because the muscles are damaged. The muscles are fine; the **impulses from the brain cannot reach them**.

fig.cap: Figure 1: A spinal cord injury. The spinal cord runs from the brain down inside the backbone. At the injury the neurones are cut or crushed and cannot regrow, so impulses cannot pass. Below the injury the person may be paralysed and lose feeling.

core.h: Limitation 2: the brain is delicate and hard to reach
core.p: The brain is soft tissue packed tightly inside the hard **skull**. To operate, surgeons must cut through the skull and often through healthy brain tissue to reach the problem. Any healthy tissue they damage may never recover.
bullets: Problems **deep inside the brain** are especially difficult because surgeons must pass through or move healthy tissue to reach them.
Areas controlling **vital functions** (for example the **medulla oblongata**, which controls breathing and heart rate) are extremely risky to operate on.
Surgery carries risks of **infection, bleeding and permanent loss of function** such as speech, movement or memory.
A treatment may successfully remove a problem but leave the patient with new disabilities, so doctors must weigh up risks and benefits.

core.p: A **tumour** is a mass of cells produced by **uncontrolled cell division**. In the brain, even a **benign** tumour (one that does not spread) can be dangerous because the **skull cannot expand**, so the tumour **presses on and damages surrounding brain tissue**. **Malignant** tumours can invade nearby tissue and spread.
bullets: Treatment options are **surgery**, **radiotherapy** (ionising radiation to kill tumour cells) and **chemotherapy** (drugs to kill dividing cells).
**Surgery**: a tumour near the surface may be removed fairly safely, but a **deep tumour** may be impossible to remove without damaging vital areas.
Tumours may grow **into** healthy tissue, so it is hard to tell where the tumour ends; leaving cells behind means it may **grow back**, while removing too much damages healthy brain.
**Radiotherapy** can also damage **healthy neurones** near the tumour, which cannot be replaced.
**Chemotherapy**: many drugs **cannot cross the blood-brain barrier**, so they cannot reach the tumour in high enough concentration.
Symptoms such as headaches, seizures or changes in behaviour depend on **which part of the brain** the tumour is pressing on.

callouts.t: Benign does not mean harmless in the brain
callouts.p: A benign tumour does not spread, but inside the rigid skull it can still **press on brain tissue** and cause serious damage or death.

fig.cap: Figure 2: The position of a brain tumour affects how easily it can be treated. A tumour near the surface may be removed with surgery, but reaching a deep tumour means cutting through healthy brain tissue, which may be damaged permanently.

core.p: The capillaries in the brain have walls that are much **less permeable** than capillaries elsewhere. This **blood-brain barrier** protects the brain from harmful substances and microorganisms in the blood, but it also **stops many medicinal drugs** from passing into brain tissue.
bullets: Small molecules the brain needs, such as **oxygen and glucose**, can still pass through.
Many drug molecules, especially large ones, **cannot cross**, so they cannot reach a tumour or diseased area in the brain.
Giving bigger doses to force more drug across increases the **side effects** on the rest of the body.
Scientists are researching ways to get drugs across, for example by injecting directly into the brain or the fluid around it, but this is invasive and risky.

callouts.p: The specialised, tightly sealed walls of the capillaries in the brain that control which substances pass from the blood into brain tissue, stopping many drugs from entering the brain.

fig.cap: Figure 3: The blood-brain barrier. Small molecules the brain needs, such as oxygen and glucose, can pass from the capillary into brain tissue, but many larger drug molecules are blocked, so drugs struggle to reach a brain tumour or diseased area.

core.h: Limitation 4: the brain is complex and not fully understood
core.p: The brain contains around **86 billion neurones**, each connected to thousands of others. Scientists still do not fully understand how many functions, such as memory or consciousness, are produced. Many functions involve **several areas working together**, so it is hard to predict exactly what a treatment will do.
bullets: It can be hard to tell **exactly which area** is responsible for a symptom, so it is hard to target treatment.
The same treatment may affect people differently because brains differ.
Drugs that change brain chemistry can have **unexpected side effects** on mood, sleep or thinking.
Many brain diseases (such as **Alzheimer's** and **Parkinson's**) have **no cure**; current drugs only slow them down or treat symptoms.
Testing new brain treatments is difficult and slow because of the risks to patients and the ethical issues involved.

callouts.p: CT and PET scans help locate damage, but they show structure or activity, not the detailed wiring, so they cannot tell doctors everything they need to know.

core.p: Exam questions often give a scenario and ask why a treatment may not work. Use this table to match each treatment to its limitation.
bullets: Always link a limitation to a **reason**: neurones do not regrow, healthy tissue is in the way, the blood-brain barrier, or the brain's complexity.
Rehabilitation (physiotherapy, speech therapy) helps the patient adapt and helps other brain areas take over, but does not replace lost neurones.

core.h: Future treatments: stem cells and research
core.p: Because neurones are not replaced naturally, scientists are researching ways to **replace damaged nervous tissue**. **Stem cells** can divide and differentiate into other cell types, including neurones, so they might one day repair spinal cords or replace neurones lost in diseases like Parkinson's.
bullets: Trials have tried transplanting stem cells into damaged spinal cords and brains, with some early promise but **no reliable cure yet**.
**Risks**: transplanted stem cells might divide uncontrollably and form **tumours**; donor cells may be **rejected** by the immune system; viruses could be transferred.
**Ethical issues**: embryonic stem cells come from embryos that are destroyed, which some people object to.
Other research includes electronic implants that bridge damaged spinal cords and new ways to deliver drugs across the blood-brain barrier.
Research is slow because it is hard to test treatments safely on the human brain.

callouts.t: Stem cells are research, not routine
callouts.p: In exam answers describe stem cell treatment for nervous system damage as a **possible future treatment** with risks, not as a proven cure.

core.h: Effects of damage depend on location
core.p: Because different parts of the nervous system have different jobs, the same type of damage can cause very different symptoms depending on where it is. This also affects whether treatment is possible.
bullets: Damage to areas of the **cerebrum** may affect speech, memory, vision, personality or voluntary movement.
Damage to the **cerebellum** affects balance and coordination.
Damage to the **medulla oblongata** can stop breathing or disrupt heart rate and is often fatal; it is too risky for most surgery.
Spinal injury high in the **neck** can paralyse arms, legs and breathing muscles; lower injuries may affect only the legs.
Damage to a **peripheral nerve** (for example in an arm) affects only the area it supplies and has a better chance of slow recovery.

core.p: Decisions about treating the nervous system are rarely simple, and 6-mark questions may ask you to weigh them up.
bullets: **Risk versus benefit**: an operation might extend life but cause loss of speech or movement; patients and doctors must decide together.
**Consent**: a patient with brain damage may not be able to give informed consent.
**Cost**: long-term care and rehabilitation for paralysis or dementia is very expensive.
**Experimental treatments**: patients with no other options may want to try unproven treatments, but these may cause harm.
**Quality of life**: treatment may aim to manage symptoms and maintain quality of life rather than to cure.

callouts.p: Give the limitations with reasons, mention a possible new treatment with its risks, and finish with a balanced judgement.

core.p: This is an explain-the-limitations point. Marks come from linking each limitation to a biological reason.
bullets: **Neurones**: do not divide / do not regrow, so damage is permanent.
**Access**: brain is inside the skull and deep areas are surrounded by healthy tissue that would be damaged.
**Blood-brain barrier**: many drugs cannot pass from blood into brain tissue.
**Complexity**: many interconnected neurones and not fully understood, so it is hard to know exactly where to treat and what the effects will be.
**Spinal injury**: impulses cannot pass the damaged point, so paralysis and loss of feeling below it.

callouts.p: Writing the brain is complicated scores little on its own. Say **why**: neurones cannot be replaced, healthy tissue is in the way, or drugs cannot cross the blood-brain barrier.

analogy.p: The spinal cord is like the main **fibre-optic cable** connecting a control centre (the brain) to every building in a city (the body). If a digger cuts the cable, every building beyond the break loses contact, even though the buildings themselves are fine, just as muscles below a spinal injury are healthy but receive no impulses. In a city you could splice the cable back together; in the CNS the neurones **cannot regrow or be rejoined**, so the break stays. A brain tumour is like a burst water main deep under the city centre: digging down to fix it means tearing up streets and buildings above (healthy brain tissue), and the city's security gates (the blood-brain barrier) stop most repair vans (drugs) driving in. Where it breaks down: real cables carry one signal along one path, whereas brain function relies on huge networks, and sometimes other parts of the brain can slowly take over a lost job.

terms.d: The brain and spinal cord.
The nerves that connect the central nervous system to the rest of the body.
A nerve cell that carries electrical impulses.
Bundle of neurones running inside the vertebral column, carrying impulses between the brain and the body.
The backbone; a chain of bones (vertebrae) that protects the spinal cord.
Loss of the ability to move muscles, for example because impulses cannot reach them from the brain.
A mass of cells formed by uncontrolled cell division.
A tumour that does not spread to other parts of the body; in the brain it can still press on and damage tissue.
A cancerous tumour that can invade neighbouring tissue and spread to other parts of the body.
Tightly sealed capillary walls in the brain that stop many substances, including many drugs, passing from the blood into brain tissue.
Treatment using ionising radiation to kill tumour cells; it can also kill nearby healthy cells.
Treatment using drugs that kill dividing cells such as cancer cells.
An undifferentiated cell that can divide and differentiate into other types of cell, possibly including neurones.
Regrowth or replacement of damaged tissue; very limited for neurones in the CNS.
Brain damage caused when the blood supply to part of the brain is interrupted.
Therapy such as physiotherapy or speech therapy that helps a person recover or adapt after damage.

mistakes.w: Spinal injuries can be fixed by surgery to join the nerves back together.
mistakes.r: Neurones in the spinal cord cannot regrow, so a severed spinal cord cannot currently be repaired; surgery only stabilises the spine.

mistakes.w: Damaged neurones are replaced by mitosis like other cells.
mistakes.r: Mature neurones do not divide, so neurones lost in the brain and spinal cord are not replaced.

mistakes.w: Paralysis happens because the muscles are damaged.
mistakes.r: Muscles are healthy, but impulses from the brain cannot pass the damaged part of the spinal cord to reach them.

mistakes.w: A benign brain tumour is harmless.
mistakes.r: A benign tumour does not spread, but in the rigid skull it presses on brain tissue and can cause serious damage.

mistakes.w: Drugs cannot treat brain tumours because the brain has no blood supply.
mistakes.r: The brain has a good blood supply, but the blood-brain barrier stops many drugs passing from the capillaries into brain tissue.

mistakes.w: Surgeons can just cut out any brain tumour.
mistakes.r: Deep tumours can only be reached by damaging healthy tissue, and tumours may be hard to separate from healthy tissue.

mistakes.w: Stem cells are used to cure spinal injuries.
mistakes.r: Stem cell treatments are still being researched; they are not a reliable cure and carry risks such as tumour formation and rejection.

mistakes.w: The brain is hard to treat because it is complicated.
mistakes.r: Give the reason: it has billions of interconnected neurones, functions are not fully understood, so it is hard to know exactly where to treat or what effects treatment will have.

exam.q: Give one reason why damage to the spinal cord is usually permanent.
model: Neurones (in the CNS) do not regrow / cannot divide / are not replaced
exam.tip: Focus on the neurones, not on the bones.

exam.q: Name the barrier that stops many drugs entering the brain from the blood.
model: Blood-brain barrier
exam.tip: Learn the exact name.

exam.q: A person injures their spinal cord in a car accident. Explain why they cannot move their legs.
model: impulses from the brain cannot pass the damaged part of the spinal cord
so (motor) impulses do not reach the leg muscles / effectors
exam.tip: Mention impulses and the route they cannot travel.

exam.q: Explain why a person with a spinal injury in the neck may be more seriously affected than one with an injury lower down the back.
model: impulses cannot pass the injury to any part of the body below it
an injury higher up affects more of the body / arms, legs and possibly breathing muscles
exam.tip: Higher injury means more of the cord is cut off from the brain.

exam.q: Suggest two reasons why it is difficult to remove a tumour from deep inside the brain.
model: surgeons must cut through / damage healthy brain tissue to reach it
damaged neurones are not replaced so loss of function may be permanent
the tumour may be near areas that control vital functions
it may be hard to tell where the tumour ends / tumour may spread into healthy tissue
exam.tip: Any two different reasons.

exam.q: Explain why chemotherapy may not be an effective treatment for some brain tumours.
model: many drugs cannot cross the blood-brain barrier
so the drug does not reach the tumour cells in a high enough concentration (higher doses cause more side effects)
exam.tip: Name the barrier and say what it does.

exam.q: Explain why a benign tumour in the brain can be life-threatening.
model: the skull is rigid / cannot expand
so as the tumour grows it presses on / damages surrounding brain tissue (e.g. areas controlling vital functions)
exam.tip: Benign means does not spread, but pressure still causes damage.

exam.q: Scientists are researching the use of stem cells to treat spinal cord injuries. Describe how stem cells might help and give one risk.
model: stem cells are undifferentiated / can differentiate into neurones
they could replace damaged neurones / reconnect the spinal cord
risk: could divide uncontrollably and form a tumour / may be rejected / infection
exam.tip: Explain the property of stem cells that makes them useful.

exam.q: Explain why radiotherapy to treat a brain tumour can cause long-term problems for the patient.
model: radiation also kills / damages healthy neurones near the tumour
these neurones are not replaced so functions (e.g. memory) may be permanently affected
exam.tip: Link back to neurones not being replaced.

exam.q: Explain the limitations of treating damage and disease in the brain and nervous system.
model: neurones in the brain and spinal cord do not divide / rarely regrow so damage is often permanent
spinal injuries stop impulses passing so cause permanent paralysis / loss of sensation below the injury
brain is inside the skull and deep areas can only be reached by damaging healthy tissue
surgery near vital areas such as the medulla is very risky
the blood-brain barrier stops many drugs reaching brain tissue
radiotherapy damages healthy neurones as well as tumour cells
the brain is complex / not fully understood so it is hard to target treatment / predict effects
new treatments such as stem cells are experimental and have risks such as tumours
exam.tip: Cover several different limitations, each with its reason, and use examples (spinal injury, brain tumour).

worked.q: A patient has a tumour in the cerebellum. Doctors decide not to operate and use radiotherapy instead. Suggest reasons for their decision and explain one problem with radiotherapy.
steps: Recall the function: the cerebellum coordinates balance and muscle activity.

Reason against surgery: surgeons would have to cut through healthy tissue to reach it, and the cerebellum is close to the brain stem and medulla oblongata, which control breathing and heart rate, so surgery is very risky.
Damaged neurones are not replaced, so surgical damage could permanently affect balance and coordination.
Radiotherapy can be aimed at the tumour without cutting into the brain.
Problem: the radiation also damages healthy neurones near the tumour, which cannot be replaced, so the patient may still lose some function.
worked.ans: Surgery would risk permanent damage to healthy tissue and nearby vital areas because neurones are not replaced, so non-surgical radiotherapy was chosen. However, radiotherapy can also kill nearby healthy neurones, possibly causing permanent problems with balance or coordination.

worked.q: Two people have nerve damage. Person A cut a peripheral nerve in their arm. Person B has a severed spinal cord. Explain the difference in their likely outcomes.
steps: Identify the systems: a nerve in the arm is part of the peripheral nervous system; the spinal cord is part of the central nervous system.
Peripheral nerves can sometimes regrow slowly if the cell bodies are not damaged, so person A may regain some feeling and movement over months.
Neurones in the CNS do not regrow, so the break in person B's spinal cord is permanent.
Impulses cannot pass the injury, so person B is likely to have permanent paralysis and loss of sensation below the injury, affecting a large part of the body.
Person A's damage affects only the area supplied by that one nerve.
worked.ans: Person A may partly recover because peripheral nerves can slowly regrow and only one area is affected. Person B is likely to be permanently paralysed below the injury because CNS neurones do not regrow, so impulses can no longer pass between the brain and the lower body.
